caption, passed through `resolvedGuideSection` unchanged). The composition lives in the client
(`apps/client/src/task364-art.ts`, `GUIDE_ACTION_IMAGES`): each image is a row of tiles, each tile a
`[data-icon]` key, with a join (`+` for things used together, `→` for the hologram becoming a piece).
The six images: place-hologram (ghost ore store → solid ore store), claim-base (claim totem + clan
flag), cook-fire (campfire + stew bowl), tame-feed (Labrador sprite + dog biscuit, its favourite treat),
use-trough (feeding trough + animal feed), harness-mount (horse sprite + harness + cart kit). The panel
renders them as a `<figure>` of icon spans plus a `<figcaption>` — tiles are spans, never `<img>`, the
same rule as the section icons, inside ADR-363's modal styling (only `.guide-image` / tile / join /
caption rules were added to the guide's own stylesheet).

**Decision — the hologram tile is painted at runtime in the game's own ghost treatment.** It is the one
guide tile with no menu-icon art, so `paintGuideGhostPixels` re-runs the ore store's half-full front cell
(the ADR-357 painter) through the ghost shader's math (`packages/render/src/sprites.ts`: mix toward
green (0.3, 1.0, 0.4) by 0.68, alpha `smoothstep(0.35, 0.75, a) * 0.62` — the soft ground shadow drops
out, as in-game). `installGuideArt()` installs it as `[data-icon="guide_ghost_ore_store"]` (style
`#task364-guide-art`, ADR-357 pattern: idempotent, safe no-op without a canvas), called once in
`view.ts` next to the store/vehicle installs. The solid tile reuses the build menu's own ADR-357 icon
(`build_ore_store`): the shipped items_build frame 297 is blank (0 opaque pixels, re-asserted here), so
the painted icon is the real art. The ghost is a rendering of an existing sprite in the treatment the
game draws every placement preview in — not a new sprite.

**Verification.** New `apps/client/test/adr364_guide_art.test.ts` (8 tests): all 15 sections resolve an
icon against the shipped + runtime key sets; the pet/mount CSS values are re-derived from the manifest
(4-significant-figure match) and both atlas rects are decoded from the shipped PNGs (node:zlib pattern
from `packages/assets/test/clan_palettes.test.ts`) and non-blank at 1x and 2x; every guide image id exists
in the registry and every registry entry is used; every tile is non-blank by pixel check — atlas tiles
decoded at exactly the cell the CSS shows, runtime tiles from the painters that produce them, with
distinct signatures per tile inside each image; the ghost is pixel-identical to the solid icon except for
the ghost treatment (RGB mix within ±1, alpha from the shader ramp, green-shifted); install is
idempotent and a safe no-op without a canvas; the panel renders each image with its tiles in order, the
right join and the caption, and no `<img>` anywhere. `packages/gameplay/test/adr362_guide.test.ts`
gains the image-item validation tests (kebab-case id, digit-free caption, rejection of malformed items,
resolved passthrough) and the captions join the no-digits check; `adr363_guide_ui.test.ts` now expects
the pet/mount icons and renders image items in the all-sections sweep. Neighbours: full client suite
green (185 files, 880 tests passed); full gameplay suite green (191 files, 2006 tests passed, 3
skipped). Typecheck with pinned TypeScript 5.9.3:
`pnpm -r typecheck` clean across all 11 workspace projects (root `node_modules/@engine/gameplay`
symlink moved aside for the run, then restored). No package-name self-imports in new files (grep
confirms).

**Honest cuts.** The six action images are tile rows, not staged screenshots: they show the exact
sprites involved in each action, composed, but not a live scene of the action happening. The 39 custom
icons (`game-icons-data.ts`) and the disease/temperature HUD chips were reviewed as art sources; no
section icon or action image needed one — the atlas sprites depict the actual game objects more
directly — so they stay unused by the guide for now. The guide has no hotkey and is not on the menu
bar: it opens from the main menu or from pause only (unchanged from ADR-363).

## ADR-368: Sim hot paths — cache the repeated work, keep the outcomes (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** The busy-world sim runs ~1.5 ms/tick (Task 29 profile harness, `PERF=1`), and Task 29
already took the biggest wins (allocation-free `findPath` A*, creature-nav scratch, store-direct animal
AI, hoisted exposure ambient, bot sensor caching). What was left was the same shape of waste one level
down: per-call rebuilds of lists the hot paths read many times a tick, per-entity re-derivations of
values that are constant across a pass, and full scans for holders / animals / nodes that have nothing
to do. Nothing here changes a spawn rate, a balance number, a tuning value, or a gameplay outcome —
every change is a cache, a hoist, or a skipped no-op, with the old computation kept as the fallback.

**Decision — `inSpawnSafeRadius` merges its point lists at most once per tick.** `extraSafeSpawnPoints`
re-spread and re-copied every point (installed, dynamic, temporary) on every call, and the predicate
runs per survivor per zombie think (`acquire`), per animal with a threat (animal AI engage), and per
spawn-gate attempt. The merged list is now cached per (tick, version) in the resource; every
registration change (set / provider / temporary centre, plus lazy materialisation and temp pruning)
bumps the version so a mid-tick registration is visible to the next read in the same tick, and the
returned array is documented read-only. `inSpawnSafeRadius` also reads the installed points in place
instead of copying them. Providers are still re-evaluated at most once per tick, as ADR-348 promised.

**Decision — `findPath` records the first blocking piece while it searches.** The post-pass re-ran
`stepBlocker` over every tile of the returned path (a chunk-layer `cellsIn` per tile). The relaxation
now records the blocker of the edge into each node in a `P_BLOCKER` scratch array, set exactly when
`P_FROM` is, so it always describes the chosen path's edge; the post-pass reads it back. `stepBlocker`
is deterministic on the geometry, so blocker, blockerIndex and cost are unchanged.

**Decision — zombie `acquire` takes the tuning it already has.** It called `gameplayDefs(world).ai`
and `secondsToTicks(retaliateSeconds)` per survivor per zombie per think; the caller already holds
`ai`, and the retaliate window is computed once per call. The per-tick `paths` / `snuffs` cleanup
loops also stop spreading every key into a fresh array and delete during Map iteration instead.

**Decision — `expressionSystem` stops allocating per pass.** Emote names and expression ids are
computed once at module load (a `Map` instead of `indexOf` per entity); the four queries collect
into one reused array that is sorted and deduped in place (same deterministic order, each entity
once); `mood()` and the current-expression reads use `getField` instead of `world.get()` copies.
`emoteNames()` itself still returns a fresh array for its external callers.

**Decision — `spoilageSystem` skips the per-item work for holders with no spoilable food.** Most holders carry none, but
every pass ran `mapSlots` (which copies every slot array) for all of them. An allocation-free scan over the live slot
arrays gates the per-item decay/conversion loop; the `frozenLast` update still runs for every holder, so food added
later never inherits a stale freeze credit, and `burnSalt` keeps its salt-fuel and salt-count guards (its own
`holdsSpoilable` scan was redundant under the gate) and still only burns while food is present. The holder's
`spoilMul` still re-bases every pass even with no spoilable food — it is a property of the container, read by
`spoilMulOf` / `slotFreshness` and by transfers, and Task 28 pins it (a salt barrel holding only salt reads 0.5x);
the first draft of this slice skipped the re-base too and broke `task28_salt_storage` (gate fix, 2026-11-12).
The ambient temperature is hoisted once per pass when there is no `ClimateRes`
(the same hoist exposure got in Task 29); underground holders still read the constant 60°F, and
with a `ClimateRes` the per-holder reading stays.

**Decision — `cropGrowthSystem` hoists the pass globals and merges the frost pass.** `growthMul`
re-derived the time of day and the weather per plant, and `droughtTicks` re-read the clock per plant;
raining / sun-up / dormant / drought / frost are now computed once per pass and passed in (the live
reads remain the fallback when the caller does not pass them). The crop half of the frost kill runs
inside the growth loop instead of a second sorted query over the same crops (same order, same
per-plant outcome); only the `ResourceNode` half keeps its own pass, and only while freezing. The
growth-only write is `setField` instead of a whole-component `set` (same values, same change mark).

**Decision — `husbandrySystem` looks each animal's station up once.** `feedingTroughs` /
`apiaries` did a full `BuildPiece` query plus sort every pass, and `atTrough` / `atApiary` re-scanned
them (with a `Transform` copy per station) up to five times per animal per pass, along with
`tamedOwnerId` / `tamedOwnerTribe` / `canUsePens`. Station lists are now cached per
`StructureIndex` version (the `pieceAt` memo convention; worlds without an index scan fresh), and
each animal's trough, apiary, owner id, tribe id, kind key and pens gate are computed once per pass
and reused by grouping, eating, production and grazing.

**Decision — animal AI reuses one zombie list; `respawnSystem` stops spreading.** Tame defenders
called `nearestClaimHostile` without a list, which ran a spatial radius query per tame animal per
tick; the living-zombie list is now built once per run (lazily, on the first tame defender that
needs it) and passed in — the same exact-distance nearest rule as petSystem's Task 29 list (ties
resolve in query order rather than spatial-index order). `respawnSystem` ran every tick spreading
every `ResourceNode` and every `NodeRegrow` marker into fresh arrays to find the few due ones; it
now collects due entities into reused scratch arrays and then processes them (collection and
processing are separate passes, so destroying / creating during processing cannot disturb the
query iteration; order is the query order, as before).

**Verification.** New `packages/gameplay/test/adr368_sim_hotpaths.test.ts` (13 tests): the safe-centre
provider is evaluated at most once per tick and a mid-tick registration applies at once; temporary
centres expire; `findPath` returns the exact straight tiles with no blocker on open ground, is
deterministic across calls, and reports the wall piece `stepBlocker` reports for the crossed step
in a walled room; expression ids / emote ids resolve from the cached tables and a held mood
expression is not rewritten by repeated runs; a pack with only non-spoilable items keeps `spoilMul`
1 while spoilable fish still decays; a watered wheat crop grows at the watered rate, an unwatered
one does not, and a full-growth crop still matures into its node; a fed cow at a real placed trough
still produces milk; an amount-0 node becomes a regrow marker and then regrows, and 30 live nodes
are untouched by the per-tick scan. Neighbours (existing suites for animals, zombies, nav215,
spoilage / salt storage, crops, trough diets, spawn points, expression) are unchanged in behaviour
and must stay green. **Not run here: the sparse checkout had not landed and no `node_modules` were
available, so no vitest suite and no typecheck ran in this slice — run `pnpm --filter
@engine/gameplay test` and `pnpm bench` / `PERF=1 pnpm vitest run
packages/gameplay/test/bench215.test.ts` on a full checkout before pushing, and confirm the
busy-world sim still runs ~1.5 ms/tick or better.**

**Honest cuts.** No measured before/after numbers in this slice (checkout blocked — see above); the
wins are structural (fewer allocations and repeated scans per tick), not a re-tuned sim. Vitals was
reviewed and left alone: it is already store-direct and `evaluate` scans at most 8 modifier slots.
`findPath` still returns an allocated tile list per call, and `animalAISystem` still sorts its animal
list per tick — both are load-bearing for determinism, so they stay. The `extraSafeSpawnPoints`
merged array is shared within a tick and must be treated as read-only by callers.

## ADR-369: Net replication — cheaper ticks, same wire (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** The 2026-11-12 performance batch asked for less lag with no graphics-quality cut. The
replication path was already heavily optimised (ADR-212: structural sharing in `captureState`, the
per-(state, baseline) encoded-record cache, distance/staleness prioritisation, shared tile deltas),
so this slice takes the remaining per-tick work that scales with world/client size rather than with
churn: `captureState` re-scanned every entity against every replicated store every tick
(O(entities × stores)) even when nothing had changed; `replicate` walked the captured state three
times plus a full `posX.fill(NaN)`; every client re-walked every AOI chunk and re-resolved every
netId every tick even when its AOI set had not moved; tile/static streaming re-scored each chunk's
distance on every sort comparison; and `BitWriter.writeBytes` / `BitReader.readBytes` went through
`writeBits`/`readBits` one byte at a time.

**Decision — dirty-driven capture.** `captureState` (packages/net/src/state.ts) now builds one
`dirty` set per tick from the stores' own `changedIndices()` iterators plus the NetId store's
(O(changed)), and reuses the previous `EntityState` whenever an entity is in neither `dirty` nor
the removal (`touched`) set. That is exactly the old fast path — `changedIndices()` yields a
changed index only while the component is still present, removals are covered by `touched`, and
NetId adds by the NetId store — with the per-entity × per-store `isChanged` scan gone. The
per-component structural sharing inside a rebuilt entity is unchanged. `writeEntityRecord` also
writes the changed/removed masks with one linear merge instead of `changed.includes(ci)` per
component (the masks are built in ascending ci order, so the bits on the wire are identical).

**Decision — cached relevant netIds.** `NetServer.replicate` keeps a per-client list of the
netIds in that client's AOI, in the same order the chunk walk produces it, and reuses it while
`InterestGrid` reports no entered/left entities or chunks for that client — the grid already
maintains the relevant set incrementally, so empty deltas mean the set is unchanged. A rebuild
happens on any AOI change, on disconnect/remove, on `setDirect` either way (the grid keeps
updating while a client is direct, so a cache built before going direct is stale on return), and
whenever `NetIdRegistry.generation` moves: the registry now bumps a generation counter on every
netId assignment, adoption and release, so an entity that gains a netId while sitting still inside
a client's AOI is never missed by a stale cache. `server.perf` gains `relevantHits` /
`relevantBuilds` (reset per tick like `encoded` / `shared`) so the hit rate is observable in the
benches. One documented nuance, not a wire change: on a cache hit the list keeps the order it was
built in, so an entity moving between two chunks that are both still relevant keeps its old
position in that order. The set is identical and `prioritize()` reorders `rest` by
distance/staleness anyway, so only ties among equal distance/staleness can come out in a
different order, and no entity is dropped or delayed past the budget logic.

**Decision — one pass over the captured state.** `replicate` used to walk `cur.keys()` three
times (max id, positions, max id again) plus `posX.fill(NaN)` and a `forEach` to fill `curArr`.
It now takes one max scan and one `forEach` that fills `curArr` and `posX`/`posY` together, and
the fill is gone: every id in `cur` gets a `posX`/`posY` write in that pass, and every reader
only touches ids in `cur` (`prioritize`, distant throttle) or ids guarded by `curArr` (linger),
so no stale position can be read. The `[...st.changedIndices()]` snapshot in the NetId-assign
loop is now a direct generator iteration (assign only writes the NetId store, never the store
being iterated); the NetId store's own loop keeps its spread deliberately, because `adopt()` can
write the store being iterated.

**Decision — bulk bit copies and once-per-chunk scoring.** `BitWriter.writeBytes` and
`BitReader.readBytes` (packages/net/src/bits.ts) take a direct buffer copy when byte-aligned
(tile deltas and blobs are the hot callers), bit-identical to one `writeBits`/`readBits` per byte,
with the same overrun `RangeError`. `TileSync` (`tiles.ts`) and `StaticServer.build`
(`static.ts`) score each chunk's distance once before sorting instead of re-parsing the chunk
key and re-scanning viewpoints on every comparison — same order, same bytes. `StaticServer.update`
reuses one `seen` set instead of allocating a fresh `Set` per tick.

**Verification.** New `packages/net/test/adr369_net_replication.test.ts` (7 tests): bulk
write/read bytes are byte-identical to the per-byte path aligned and unaligned, and overruns
throw the same error; a 200-entity idle tick reuses every `EntityState`, a write to the
non-networked `Control` component changes nothing, a single `Buff` write rebuilds only that
entity while its `Transform` array is structurally shared, and a component removal is still
detected; a multi-component change + removal round-trips exactly through `encodeDelta` /
`decodeDelta`; over loopback, idle ticks report `perf.relevantHits = 1, relevantBuilds = 0`, a
move between two still-relevant chunks keeps the cache hit and the client still sees the entity,
leaving the AOI rebuilds on the next tick (`relevantBuilds = 1`) and the entity despawns past
the linger and re-spawns on re-entry, and `netIds.generation` moves on assign and on release;
tile streaming with radius 2 loads 16 chunks nearest-first (distances non-decreasing, own
chunk first). Not run here: the sparse checkout had not landed when this slice was written
(working tree held only root files), so no vitest or typecheck run was possible — see Honest
cuts for the exact commands. No wire change: protocol version stays 8, no field renamed, no
message dropped; the new tests assert byte-identical encodings and unchanged client-visible
sets, and the existing `bench` / `tiles.bench` / `stalls.bench` / `war.bench` suites are the
regression net (run them with `PERF=1`).

**Honest cuts.** Unmeasured — checkout blocked. The mechanisms above remove work that scales
with entities × stores × clients on idle/low-churn ticks and with chunks × log(chunks) ×
comparisons on streaming ticks, but no before/after number was measured in this slice; the
baselines to beat are the ones the benches already print (`bench.test.ts`: ~13 ms/tick for
100 clients × 10k entities spread, ~25 ms/tick clustered, both on the dev box). Run before
merging, from a full checkout: `pnpm --filter @engine/net test`
(or `pnpm test:net`), `pnpm -r typecheck` with the lockfile-pinned TypeScript 5.9.3, and
`pnpm bench` (`PERF=1 vitest run --no-file-parallelism packages/net/test/bench.test.ts
packages/persist/test/bench.test.ts`), plus the tile/static suites. Deliberately not changed:
the twice-per-tick `ownedBy` rebuild (the owned set is O(players), and reusing the input-phase
cache would miss entities whose `Owner` was added during simulation); the `decodeDelta`
per-Change `copyMap` on the client (needed for the immutable-state contract); the per-tick
`TileSync` leave scan over subscribed chunks (no cheap invalidation signal exists for chunk
unloads); `encodeDelta` (no hot-path caller); and anything in the wire format, snapshot
format, scopes, budgets, throttle or linger behaviour.

## ADR-370: Render warm-up — first-view atlas page-in, a bounded warm-up window (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** The first gameplay frames page stream sheets in at 2 uploads/frame, in whatever order the draw happens to request them (`AtlasManager.pump` / `PAGE_UPLOADS_PER_FRAME`, `STREAM_UPLOADS_PER_FRAME`), while the boot screen only waits for the *resident* atlases (`IsoView.create` → `setRegistry`, which pages body sheets in eagerly at prio 0). A first view with ~20 stream pages therefore spends its first ~10 frames drawing placeholders / body-only fallbacks — the blurry start — even though the art is already on disk / in the ADR-307 cache. Separately, `ChunkManager.update()` drains its load queue in row-major order, so the chunk under the player can load up to 24 chunks after the corner chunk, and there is no prewarm knob: `loadRadius` (default 2, 5×5 chunks) *is* the radius. The ready gate (`ready.ts`) already waits for the 3×3 chunk block around the player before the second loading screen lifts, and the first frames already draw under that overlay.

**Decision — atlas page-in priority for the first view.** New pure module `packages/render/src/assets/warmup.ts` (no GL/DOM/imports) orders atlas keys into tiers: 0 = an explicit first-view set, 1 = visible-pin art (`gt_` / furniture / buildings / openings / defenses — in view at almost any spawn, since spawns sit beside abandoned structures, ADR-300/325), 2 = hot art, 3 = everything else, 4 = cold / ride pages (never warmed). `AtlasManager.warmupFirstView(keys, { firstView, maxPages, timeoutMs })` requests the tier 0–1 lazy pages at `WARMUP_PRIO` 1 — ≤ `PRIO_NEAR` (16), so budget-exempt like near art, but ≠ 0, so the pages still go through the per-frame upload turn and never jump the local player's own pages — and waits, bounded (default 1500 ms, 24 pages), for them to land. It reuses `request()` / `pump()` / `pageIn`; there is no new upload path.

**Decision — warm-up window on load, in two places.** (1) Boot: `IsoView.create` runs `warmupFirstView` over the visible-pin keys right after `setRegistry`, before the "ready" stage; the result is stored on the view (`view.warmupResult`). (2) World entry: `main.ts` adds `drainFirstView()` after `waitForWorldReady` (both the menu `enterWorld` path and `signalReady`), which awaits `atlas.warmupDrain()` — the first-view pages the draws under the loading overlay already queued, draining before the overlay lifts. Both windows are bounded by `WARMUP_WINDOW_MS` (1500 ms); expiry never blocks boot or entry, it just means a soft start on a slow device.

**Decision — asset cache / prefetch (ADR-307 extension).** `collectWarmupPrefetchUrls` (asset-fetch.ts) warms the first-view *stream* sheets (visible-pin pages, including building tiers and their emissive images) in Cache Storage; `prefetch-art.ts` warms them after the resident set, so the boot warm-up's first page-in is a cache hit. The set is disjoint from `collectPrefetchUrls` (resident atlases stay there; ride pages and cold sheets stay on demand).

**Gate fix (2026-11-12): chunk prewarm dropped.** The nearest-first drain was reverted during gating: under the game's `maxLoadsPerUpdate: 4` / `maxLoadTimeMs: 2` budget it turned the fair FIFO load queue into a priority queue, and far-but-wanted chunks could starve while nearer chunks kept arriving (bots move; sources shift). The ADR-252 live bot test proved it: with the sort, one bot never placed its bed within the 3600-tick build window (night fell at the 3600-tick timeout, 0 night-sleep ticks); with the sort reverted, both bots build the bed and sleep (night at tick 3079, 502 sleep ticks). `ChunkManager` is back to pristine FIFO order and `packages/world/test/adr370_chunk_prewarm.test.ts` is removed. The atlas warm-up — the part that fixes the blurry start — is unchanged.

**Decision — client cost breakdown.** `LoadCostBreakdown` (load-progress.ts, pure) records sequential phases (`boot`, `world-ready`, `warmup-drain`) with shares of the total, plus notes for sub-timings (the boot warm-up runs inside `boot`, so it is a note, never double-counted). `main.ts` records the phases, exposes `window.__survivazLoadCost()`, and `?diag=1` prints the breakdown (`diag.ts` `loadCost` source).

**Not changed.** Full stays the default preset and full-resolution rendering (`quality.ts` untouched); no resolution, mip-level, texture-quality, bloom or lighting change; compass untouched; no new art, recolors, or binary art; `BOOT_STAGES` weights and the loading bar are untouched; `ChunkManager` load radius, cache size, unload margin and load order are untouched; `chunkFadeIn` (0.35 s) is untouched.

**Validation.** New `packages/render/test/adr370_warmup.test.ts` (pure ordering + tier agreement with the AtlasManager's own regexes + warm-up prefetch disjointness + stubbed-manager warm-up/drain/key tests) and `apps/client/test/adr370_load_cost.test.ts` (breakdown totals, shares, notes, invalid-input handling). The chunk-prewarm test (`packages/world/test/adr370_chunk_prewarm.test.ts`) was removed with the reverted sort — see the gate fix above. Not run in this slice: the sparse checkout was still downloading (working tree held root files only), so no vitest / typecheck run was possible here — the coordinator must run `pnpm --filter @engine/render test -- adr370_warmup`, `pnpm --filter @engine/world test -- adr370_chunk_prewarm`, the client suite, and `pnpm -r typecheck` after applying, and measure the first-view page-in drain in `perfMobile.mjs` (warm-up resident count + `vram.misses` over the first seconds) before claiming a speedup.

**Honest cuts.** The boot warm-up set is spawn-independent (visible-pin keys); the spawn-*specific* pages (crops, animals, furniture actually at the spawn) are covered only by the world-entry drain, because the spawn tile is not known until the player spawns. Tier 0 (explicit first-view set) is plumbed through `warmupFirstView({ firstView })` and `warmupKeysForSprites()` for a future spawn-aware caller, but no caller passes one yet. No live visual verification was possible in this slice: the blurry start still needs user eyes on a real phone and desktop.

## ADR-371: Vehicle passengers — ride and destination dismount (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** Tracey asked (2026-11-12) for players and AI humans to ride in the passenger seats of wagons,
carriages and carts while another player or AI human drives, and to dismount when their destination is reached —
with no performance drop. Most of it already existed and was verified, not assumed: drawn defs already carry
passenger seats (wagon_small/medium/large + covered: 2, cart: 2, carriage: 4, chariot: 2); `VehicleSeats` /
`Driver` / `enterVehicle` / `validateEnter` already seat passengers (seat 255 = first free, passengers need no
key, seat 0 needs the key); `vehicleSystem` already snaps *every* rider — driver or passenger — to the vehicle
Transform each tick, so drawn-vehicle passenger follow needed no new code; a passenger's input already moves
nothing (ADR-360 test); and ADR-360 driver-seat steering of the pulling mount already works. The real gaps were
four: no way to board *as a passenger* when you hold the key (seat 255 takes the driver seat first); the
dismount dropped the rider on a fixed left-side point with no safety check (inside a solid, a wall, or deep
water); no AI passenger behaviour at all; and a rider whose vehicle entity vanished was left frozen with a
dangling `Driver` (the old `vehicleSystem` early-returned when no vehicles remained, so the follow loop never
ran to notice).

**Decision — seat 254, the passenger seat.** `PASSENGER_SEAT = 254` in `packages/gameplay/src/vehicles.ts`
means first free *passenger* seat (1..n-1), never seat 0. `validateEnter` / `enterVehicle` handle it alongside
255 (new reasons: `full` when no passenger seat is free, `no_passenger_seats` on a single-seat vehicle), and
`enterVehicleAsPassenger` / `firstFreePassengerSeat` / `vehicleHasDriver` expose it. The command is the same
`gameplay.vehicleEnter` (no new command, no wire change — the seat is a `u8` payload), so bots already speak it:
`venter:<vehicle>:254` passes through `agent_output.ts` untouched. Chariot is included: it shares the seats /
hitch / drive code path exactly, so excluding it would have been an artificial carve-out.

**Decision — safe dismount, never strand a passenger.** `exitVehicle` now places the rider through
`findSafeDismountTile` (same file): first the legacy left-side point (width/2 + 0.6 — the ADR-360 spot, so the
existing exit tests pass unchanged on open ground), then tile centres on expanding Chebyshev rings around the
vehicle tile, nearest the legacy point first, outside the vehicle footprint, checked with `movementBlocked`
(terrain, walls/doors, solid cells at the rider's level). Land and shallow water are tried first; deep water
only on a second pass — a ground-level rider can swim out, but wading out beats swimming out. Radii live in
data, not code: `packages/gameplay/data/vehicle_passengers.json`
(`dismountSearchRadiusTiles: 3`, `dismountFallbackRadiusTiles: 6`). The fallback, in order: another adjacent
tile; the fallback radius (forced exits only); and, when even that finds nothing, the rider stays exactly where
they already stand — never moved onto an unchecked tile. A normal exit with no safe tile inside the search
radius returns `no_safe_spot` and the rider *stays seated* (seat and `Driver` kept) to retry later, when the
vehicle has moved on or a tile frees up. Exiting a moving vehicle still works (the ADR-360 exit-while-driving
case): the spot is found at the current pose. A driver leaving, or a mount being unhitched, leaves passengers
seated in the parked vehicle — that *is* the safe place; they exit on demand, and the AI behaviour below exits
when its driver has left. No in-sim path destroys a vehicle entity today (wrecked vehicles persist and are
repairable, and the ADR-360 wreck test — the driver stays seated in a wreck — is preserved), so destruction is
covered two ways: `forceExitVehicle` / `ejectVehicleOccupants` (O(seats), the API a future destroy path must
call) and a safety net in `vehicleSystem`, which now ejects dangling riders — including when no vehicles remain
at all, the early-return case the old code missed.

**Decision — AI passenger.** New behaviour `ride_passenger` (`packages/gameplay/src/ai/vehicle_behaviors.ts`,
appended last so the `vehicle_craft.test.ts` positional destructuring of `[drive, vehicle_service]` is
untouched): it boards a driven drawn vehicle (`pickPassengerRide`: parked, driver seated, a free passenger
seat, within the existing `seekRadius`) when far from its own goal, claims the tick and does nothing while
riding (a passenger's input moves nothing), and gets out when parked and (a) the vehicle is within
`arriveDistance` of its goal, (b) the driver has left, (c) the wagon is wrecked, or (d) the ride has carried it
10 tiles further from its goal than where it boarded (wrong way). Sensors grew two O(seats) fields
(`SeenVehicle.driverSeated`, `freePassengerSeats`, read in `fillVehicleSensors`); `mount_behaviors.ts`
`DISMOUNT_NOW` gained `ride_passenger` so a bot on its own mount gets off it before boarding (enter refuses a
rider who is already riding). While riding, the "far" consideration stays true: the utility product in
`scoreBehavior` zeroes a behaviour the moment any consideration is 0, so a threshold that flips at arrival
would let another behaviour displace the passenger before it can dismount. Motor vehicles are out of scope —
the existing `drive` behaviour already exits non-driver riders from them, and that was left alone.

**Decision — player UX, no new bindings.** The client (`apps/client/src/vehicle-controls.ts`) sends the
passenger intent (seat 254) on Interact when the nearest drawn vehicle already has a driver, and the drive
intent (seat 255) otherwise — a driverless wagon still needs somebody to drive it. While riding as a passenger
the HUD chip reads "Passenger · Interact to get off"; the driver chip is unchanged (hidden for drawn vehicles,
ADR-360). Boarding and dismounting both go through Interact (E / pad X / touch "Use"), so keyboard, gamepad
and touch all work with no new binding, no new button, and no touch-layout change; the compass is untouched.
The one wart, inherited not introduced: the touch driving layout still shows Engine/Lights buttons to a drawn
passenger, and they do nothing (the server rejects them — driver only). No new art, no new component (the
world schema hash is still `0xb629eab2`), no gameplay or balance change beyond the ask.

**Validation.** New `packages/gameplay/test/adr371_vehicle_passengers.test.ts` (26 tests, all passing): seat-254
boarding, key-holder passenger protection, single-seat `no_passenger_seats`, carriage seat tracking, chariot
inclusion, passenger follow while moving, passenger input moves nothing, legacy-spot dismount, blocked-legacy
fallback (lake shore: deep refused, shallow taken), deep water as last resort, `findSafeDismountTile`
undefined when the only candidate is unsafe, walled-in `no_safe_spot` stays seated, driver-leaves and
unhitch leave passengers seated, `ejectVehicleOccupants`, destroyed-vehicle ejection on the next tick,
exiting an already-gone vehicle, the `ride_passenger` registry entry and pick rules, a full two-bot ride
(passenger boards, rides, dismounts at the shared goal), driver-leaves dismount, wrong-way dismount, staying
seated while rolling, schema hash, tuning validation, and the `vehicleInteractCommand` passenger form. New
`apps/client/test/adr371_passenger_controls.test.ts` (6 tests): the 254/255 intents, Interact boarding as
passenger / driver / motor-vehicle, the passenger chip, and the unchanged driver chip. Neighbours re-run
green: `vehicles`, `adr358`, `adr360`, `vehicle_keys`, `vehicle_craft`, `vehicle_net`, `vehicle_state`,
`adr319_mounts`, `adr321_ai_mounts`, and the ADR-360 client render suite. Typecheck passes with the
lockfile-pinned TypeScript 5.9.3 (`pnpm --filter @engine/gameplay typecheck`).

**Performance.** No per-tick allocations in hot paths, no new per-tick scans: seat-follow is the existing
O(riders) loop, the dangling-rider check piggybacks on it (one O(1) map lookup per rider), the sensor seat
read is O(seats) per seen vehicle inside the existing sensor scan, and the dismount search is O(local tiles)
on exit only. Bench (`PERF=1`, same VM, `packages/gameplay/test/bench215.test.ts`, median of 3): before —
open 2.582 ms/tick, base 7.741 ms/tick; after — open 1.389 ms/tick, base 4.205 ms/tick. No speedup is
claimed: the slice adds behaviour, it does not optimise the sim, and this shared VM is noisy — the after-run's
own base spread was 2.510–5.225 ms/tick across its three rounds, overlapping the before-run's 5.834–7.990, and
the bench scenario contains no vehicles at all, so it cannot measure this slice's cost either way; the numbers
are reported so a regression would show. `pnpm bench` (net + persist) was run after-only: net spread 18.6 /
clustered 42.37 ms/tick, persist autosave p95 1.61–1.77 ms — it failed once on the first run (persist p95
10.45 ms vs the 2.5 ms ceiling) and passed on a clean re-run with no code change, i.e. VM noise, not this
slice (it touches neither net nor persist).

**Honest cuts.** Not verified live: a real two-player ride (one drives, one rides) on a phone and desktop, the
passenger chip on touch, and a passenger dismounting onto a crowded / built-up tile in a real base — Tracey's
eyes on the live build are the check. A bot only boards a wagon whose driver is already seated; it never
waits beside a driverless wagon for a driver to show up, and it cannot tell where the driver is headed, so a
ride can overshoot the passenger's goal (the wrong-way rule only fires once parked, 10+ tiles worse than
boarding). A passenger whose wagon parks 7–25 tiles short of their goal with the driver still seated stays
seated — the ride has not ended, it is just paused. `vehicleInteractCommand` gained an `asPassenger` option
but no other caller uses it yet. Deliberately not changed: motor-vehicle passengers (`drive` already exits
non-drivers there), exit-while-moving (kept — ADR-360 depends on it), eject-on-wreck (kept — the wrecked
wagon's driver stays seated by the motor rule), and anything in the wire format, the seat anchors, or the
render placement of riders.

## ADR-372: Stairs and second-floor access (SurVivaZ)

> Apply order: this entry follows ADR-371 (passengers) in the batch — the gate agent applies 371, then 372, then 373. All three append after ADR-370; this hunk overlaps ADR-371's append.

**Context.** The abandoned generator already placed internal `stairs` pieces (role `stair`) and level-1 floors with a `floor_stairwell` hole in its five two-story+ kinds (TwoStoryCottage, TwoStoryFarmhouse, TwoStoryHomestead, Townhouse, Manor), but no code ever moved an entity between levels on them: `standHeightAt` knew decks and foundations, `findPath` was a level-0-only A*, and `walkerWaypoint` hardcoded level 0. There were no outside stairs at all, and no way for a missing stair to be rebuilt into a climbable route. The player building system already supports upper levels (wall-supported decks validate; pillar-only decks do not, by the existing `deckWallConnected` rule) and the claim-build planner (ADR-337) already rebuilds missing structural pieces — both are reused, not replaced.

**Decision — a stair tile is a ramp in `standHeightAt`.** New pure module `packages/gameplay/src/building/stairs.ts` (`stairRampHeight`, `stairUpDir`, `stairPieceAt`, `stairLinkUp/Down`, `stairLandingAt`, data in `packages/gameplay/data/stairs.json`): when an entity stands on a stair tile, stand height is `level * levelHeight + frac * levelHeight`, where `frac` is progress 0..1 across the tile toward the top edge (`0.5 + dot(pos - centre, upDir)`, clamped). Walking up raises z at the existing `stepRate` (6/s); walking back down lowers it; `settleStandZ` eases both ways, so stopping mid-flight, turning back, or stepping off sideways settles onto the nearest level instead of sticking. The ramp lives in `standHeightAt`, so every mover that settles climbs the same way — players and AI humans via `applyMovementInput`, creatures via `creatureStep`, zombies via their step — by walking, with no button and no UI, on keyboard, gamepad and touch alike. The up direction is a data knob (`upDir: [0,-1]`, rot 0 → north, rotated by the same basis that rotates site layouts). The up-ramp applies only if a landing exists one level up: a non-roof deck on the stair tile itself (the `floor_stairwell` hole) or on the tile past the top edge (outside balcony). No landing → no ramp. A stair tile is a ramp across its whole tile — stepping onto it from any side puts you on the ramp, and crossing it sideways still carries you up; there are no stuck states, and that trade-off was accepted over a z/direction gate, which would oscillate (the ramp rises 8.7/s at walk speed vs the 6/s ease). Two flights stacked on one tile are NOT supported: the upper flight shadows the way back down (up-ramp wins; climb to L2 works, descent on that tile does not — demolish the upper flight, or put the next flight on an adjacent tile, as the Townhouse does).

**Decision — outside stairs.** `exteriorStairsFor` (`stairs.json`: `exteriorKinds` = two_story_cottage, two_story_farmhouse, townhouse) adds, on the south side in local coords, a balcony tile B (foundation + pillar + level-1 floor) and a stair tile A one row further south (foundation + stairs, rot 0, up = north, marked `exterior: true`), plus a level-1 south-wall doorway at the balcony column (`walls()` gains a `doorI?` param); the site grows 2 rows. Homestead and Manor are excluded (south pen-yard conflict) and keep interior stairs only. The Townhouse's second flight moves to its own tile (`sx+1, sy` at level 1, with the level-2 `floor_stairwell` above it) because of the stacked-flight limitation above. `rotateBuilt` now preserves rot for role `stair` (it used to zero it), so a rotated site's stair run still climbs toward its landing. Furniture is moved off stair tiles (Cottage/Homestead/Manor wardrobe one tile east; Townhouse L2 storage one tile east) and random extras never land on a stair tile (a `cook_range` used to spawn on the Townhouse flight).

**Decision — broken / missing stairs are ruin-scaled and deterministic.** `planAbandonedSite` rolls on its own seeded stream `rng(hashU32(seed, ox, oy, 0x5A172))`, so the main plan stream (layouts, loot, furnishing) is untouched: the interior ground flight is omitted iff `roll < brokenChance (0.25) * ruin`; the exterior flight iff `roll < brokenExteriorChance (0.2) * ruin`. A ruin-0 site never loses its stairs (preserves the ADR-300 tests). Only the ground flight goes missing; omission is `omit=true` on the planned stair piece, so the stamp skips it, `ruinLayout` reports it missing (structural), and `planClaimRuin` rebuilds it — no new AI build behaviour. Damaged-but-present stairs remain climbable (damaged ≠ broken). If both flights on one site spawn missing (probability ≈ `brokenChance × brokenExteriorChance × ruin²`), the upper floor is unreachable until a stair is built.

**Decision — level-aware pathfinding, same pathfinders.** `findPath` (`combat/path.ts`) state is now `(x, y, level)` with optional `opts { startLevel, goalLevel, allowStairs }`; stair vertical links cost `pathStairCost` (2, from data); the heuristic adds `|level - goalLevel| * stairCost`; `PathResult` gains parallel `levels: number[]`; `stepBlocker` gains a `level = 0` param. The default (no opts) is bit-identical to the old level-0 search — `zombies.ts` is unchanged, so zombies do not route upstairs (deliberate, no balance change) — and the ADR-368 blocker-recording optimisation is preserved (the blocker scan now keys by `(x, y, level)`). `creature_nav.route()` is level-aware the same way (scratch arrays × 3 levels, `maxPathLevel` 2); `NavState` gains `lvl`/`glvl` and re-plans when the entity's level flips; the straight-sight shortcut only applies when `goalLevel === level`; `walkerWaypoint` derives the start level from `Transform.z` (was hardcoded 0) and takes an optional `goalLevel` (default = start level; existing callers unchanged). `movementBlocked` needed no change — stairs and `floor_stairwell` are not solid.

**Performance.** Stair checks are O(local tiles) only: `stairRampHeight` reuses the layer-1 cell lookup the foundation ramp already does in `standHeightAt`, the below-stairs lookup runs only above ground level, and landing `deck()` lookups run only when a stairs piece is present. No per-tick allocations in hot paths, no new per-tick scans over all entities. Benches (PERF=1, same VM, single runs): `bench215` ms/tick median of 3 — open 1.384 → 1.509, base 2.923 → 3.185 (run ranges overlap almost completely: open 0.677–1.661 vs 0.738–1.750, base 2.107–3.510 vs 2.144–4.067); `bodyAxisMove x2 + settleStandZ` 2.44 → 2.38 µs/call, `stepBlocker` 0.52 → 0.47 µs/call, `idx.cell` 0.23 → 0.24 µs/call — the hot-path micros that touch this slice are flat. No speedup is claimed. See the slice REPORT.md ("Real-play performance note (2026-11-12)"): Tracey reports the game is slow and laggy in real play since 9ecf1388, which these benches did not capture — bench numbers here must not be read as proof of real-play smoothness, and that note lists this slice's touch-points with ADR-368/369/370 for the follow-up investigation (after this batch is pushed and CI is green).

**Validation.** New `packages/gameplay/test/adr372_stairs.test.ts`, 15/15 passing (run 3×, no flakes): ramp stand heights across the tile and back down; idle on a stair settles mid-ramp; stair tiles do not block movement at either level; player walks up interior stairs to L1 and back down; outside stairs carry the player to the balcony; every two-story kind plans a usable interior flight; Townhouse second flight on its own tile with L2 stairwell; a ruined site can spawn with the ground flight missing (never at ruin 0); a missing stair blocks access until the player builds it back; player-built stairs + upper floor in a 3×3 walled room; `findPath` routes across levels via the interior stair tile when allowed and stays level 0 otherwise; an AI human walks across levels via `walkerWaypoint`; an AI human cannot route upstairs when the stairs are missing; a claiming AI human rebuilds a missing stair through the existing claim-build plan; ground-level movement unchanged. Regression: 11 targeted suites, 120/120 (adr125, adr127, adr273, adr300, adr301, adr310, adr311, adr337 ×2, adr368, nav215). Typecheck clean with lockfile-pinned TypeScript 5.9.3. Two pre-existing behaviours found while testing and left alone: the stamp never places 5 L1 corner pieces (2 floors, 3 walls) on a TwoStoryCottage — verified identical on pristine base — and the claim-build plan skips a rebuild candidate whose grid cell is still Occupied until `structureIndexSystem` runs on a world step after the destroy (the test steps the world, as real play does).

**Not changed.** No new art (stairs/floor/pillar sprites already exist; the `stairs` prefix is already in the render warm-up allowlist, so no new atlas page-in); no UI changes; compass untouched; no graphics-quality change; no new systems; `GameDefs`/`loadDefs` untouched (data is imported directly, as elsewhere); no gameplay/balance change beyond stairs; ground-level movement for entities not using stairs is unchanged; mounted riders cannot use stairs (pre-existing `rideClearanceBlocked` under a level-1 deck); ad-hoc "build stairs to chase someone upstairs" AI behaviour does not exist — bots rebuild missing stairs only as part of claiming/rebuilding a ruin, as with any piece.

**Honest cuts.** Stairs art orientation (`upDir`, rot 0 → north) is a data guess — the sprite files are not in the sparse checkout, so the climb direction still needs Tracey's eyes on the live build; if the sprite ascends the other way, flip `upDir` in `stairs.json`, not code. The ramp-across-the-whole-tile quirk and the stacked-flight limitation (above) are accepted trade-offs of the stateless ramp. No live visual verification was possible in this slice.

## ADR-373: Abandoned structures — more variety, a few more sites (SurVivaZ)

**Apply order note.** This entry is appended after the ADR-370 tail in the patch, but in
apply order it follows ADR-371 (passengers) and ADR-372 (stairs): the gate agent applies
371, then 372, then 373, and this entry lands after ADR-372's entry. Expected tail text
after all three apply: `... ADR-372 ...` followed by this `## ADR-373: Abandoned structures
— more variety, a few more sites (SurVivaZ)` entry, ending with the "Honest cuts" paragraph
below. This patch's `docs/DECISIONS.md` hunk and its `packages/gameplay/src/building/abandoned.ts`
hunk both overlap ADR-372's (both append after ADR-370; both touch `abandoned.ts`) — that is
expected; resolve by applying in order.

**Context.** The abandoned generator (ADR-300/301/311) had 14 kinds and stamped one site per
chunk with probability `SITE_CHANCE = 0.12`. The world felt samey: the same sheds, cottages
and homesteads everywhere. Tracey asked for greatly expanded variety and a few more sites,
with no performance drop. All new kinds are composed from the existing `house()` / `yard()` /
`furnished()` helpers and piece keys already in `packages/gameplay/data/pieces.json` — no new
art, no new helpers, no new systems.

**Decision — fourteen new kinds (14 → 28).** New `AbandonedKind` ids 14–27, in this order:
Mill, Schoolhouse, Chapel, TradingPost, Smithy, Bakery, Stable, Watchtower, Bathhouse, Inn,
Apiary, Granary, FisherHut, Barracks. Each has a footprint, stories, roof style, room plan,
furniture/loot placement and a `KIND_WEIGHTS` entry, following the existing patterns exactly
(same helpers, same determinism from seed — plans are a pure function of seed + origin).
The largest new kind is the Stable at 6×9, the same shape as the Barn, so every kind still
fits the `planAbandonedChunk` margin (`w+4 <= 32`, `h+4 <= 32`). The Inn is the only new
two-story kind (6×5, beds upstairs); the Watchtower's tower piece is ground-placed beside a
3×3 hut (like the HunterShack's outside campfire); the Apiary's apiaries stand inside its
fenced garden; the Stable and Bathhouse reuse the Barn/Homestead yard pattern (pen / garden).

| Kind | Footprint | Stories | Garden / Pen | Signature pieces | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shed | 3×3 | 1 | – | storage | 12 |
| Cottage | 5×5 | 1 | – | bed, table, fireplace | 12 |
| Homestead | 13×9 | 1 | garden + pen | garden beds, trough | 11 |
| Farmhouse | 7×5 | 1 | – | dining table, large chest | 8 |
| Workshop | 5×4 | 1 | – | workbench, anvil extra | 8 |
| Cabin | 4×4 | 1 | – | bed, table, lamp | 8 |
| Barn | 6×9 | 1 | pen | trough, barrels | 7 |
| HunterShack | 4×5 | 1 | – | bed, campfire outside | 6 |
| LargeHomestead | 13×10 | 1 | garden + pen | – | 6 |
| TwoStoryCottage | 5×5 | 2 | – | upstairs bed | 7 |
| TwoStoryFarmhouse | 7×5 | 2 | – | upstairs double bed | 5 |
| TwoStoryHomestead | 13×9 | 2 | garden + pen | upstairs bed | 5 |
| Townhouse | 4×5 | 3 | – | beds on levels 1–2 | 3 |
| Manor | 13×10 | 2 | garden + pen | – | 2 |
| **Mill** | 6×5 | 1 | – | workbench, crop_store, stone_store | 4 |
| **Schoolhouse** | 6×4 | 1 | – | desk_rustic, bookcase_rustic | 3 |
| **Chapel** | 5×6 | 1 | – | bench pews, statue | 3 |
| **TradingPost** | 6×5 | 1 | – | counter_rustic, stall_booth | 4 |
| **Smithy** | 5×4 | 1 | – | anvil, furnace, tool_bench | 4 |
| **Bakery** | 5×4 | 1 | – | clay_oven, cook_range, pantry | 4 |
| **Stable** | 6×9 | 1 | pen | feeding troughs | 4 |
| **Watchtower** | 6×3 | 1 | – | watchtower piece | 2 |
| **Bathhouse** | 9×5 | 1 | garden | fountain | 2 |
| **Inn** | 6×5 | 2 | – | dining table, upstairs beds | 3 |
| **Apiary** | 9×3 | 1 | garden | apiary ×2 | 3 |
| **Granary** | 5×4 | 1 | – | crop/ore/log/stick stores | 4 |
| **FisherHut** | 4×5 | 1 | – | basket, campfire outside | 3 |
| **Barracks** | 6×4 | 1 | – | bunk_bed ×2 | 3 |

**Decision — density up a little, not doubled.** `SITE_CHANCE` 0.12 → **0.15** (same exported
const in `abandoned.ts`, where the knob already lived). A chunk is 32×32 = 1024 tiles, so the
expected count goes 12 → 15 sites per 100 chunks (+25%), 12 → 15 per 10×10-chunk region
(320×320 tiles), ~117 → ~146 per 1M tiles (~977 chunks) — before terrain / near-spawn / busy
skips, which only lower the realised count. The fourteen old weights are unchanged (they
summed to 100); the new kinds add 46, so the catalogue total is 146 and each old kind's share
of sites is scaled by 100/146 while keeping its relative order — the new kinds together take
46/146 (~31%) of sites. `KIND_WEIGHTS` is now exported so tests can pin the table.

**Decision — small extensions in the existing shape.** `extrasFor` gains one or two chance
extras per new kind (existing keys, inside the footprint); `roofWeights` leans Chapel /
Schoolhouse to gable and Mill / Stable to barn roofs, and the Inn joins the two-story roof
case; `STONE_KINDS` gains Chapel, Inn and TradingPost (tier-2 stone read, same 35% roll).
Loot tables, reclaim values, claim code and the `AbandonedSite` marker are untouched; no
existing kind id, key, weight or footprint changed, so saves, reclaim and the ADR-337 / ADR-340
bot logic keep working — new kinds flow through `planAbandonedChunk` / `stampAbandonedChunk` /
`catalogHas` generically, including the AI spawn points beside abandoned sites.

**Not used, and why.** `market_counter` is not in any new kind: it carries `stall.clanOnly`,
and `validatePlacement` rejects clan-only stall pieces for the worldgen builder
(`NoPrivilege`), so it could never stamp — the TradingPost uses `counter_rustic` (same
counter shape, no stall land rules) plus `stall_booth` (no `clanOnly`, stamps fine). No
edge-placement pieces (`weapon_rack`, `map_board`, `shield_mount`) are used in any new kind:
they need a wall socket the planner does not guarantee. No windmill/sawmill kind: there is no
millstone or saw piece in `pieces.json`, and a mill made of crates would read as a warehouse,
so the Mill is a grain store instead.

**Performance.** Stamping is chunk-load-time only — no per-tick code was added, no new scans.
Measured on this VM (shared 1.5-CPU box, noisy): planning 1600 chunks 14.4 ms before
(189 sites at 0.12) vs 2.8–26.7 ms after (226 sites at 0.15); stamping 40 sites 494 ms
before vs 283 / 478 / 678 ms after (39 stamped, ~3600 pieces) — the same noisy band, no
measurable cost; per-site stamp cost is ~7–17 ms of chunk-load time, unchanged in shape.
`pnpm bench` (`PERF=1`, net + persist) fails the same thresholds before and after on this VM
(net spread 31.9 → 47.6 ms/tick, clustered 90.1 → 74.2, both over the 30 ms/tick bar;
persist autosave p95 ~5–10 ms vs the 2.5 bar; the 3000-piece chunk encode reads 1.01 ms in
one pristine run and 1.19 / 7.80 ms in two identical after-runs), so the bench numbers are
VM noise, not a regression — and the net bench does not import gameplay at all. No speedup
is claimed.

**Validation.** New `packages/gameplay/test/adr373_abandoned_variety.test.ts` (8 tests): 28
kinds with unique keys and ids 0–27, old ids/keys unchanged; weights sum to 146 with old
weights untouched and every kind reached in 5000 seeded draws; every new kind plans
deterministically with valid footprints, resolvable piece keys inside the footprint, walls /
door / top-story roof, and its signature furniture, and stamps it from real pieces; old kinds
still plan as before (Shed: 9 foundations); `SITE_CHANCE` is 0.15 and a 1600-chunk sweep
plans 226 sites (range 190–290); no two sites overlap in a 16×16-chunk plan sweep or a
6×6-chunk stamp sweep. Neighbouring suites pass: adr300 / adr301 / adr311 / adr337 /
adr340 / adr348 / modular_building, 97 tests. `pnpm --filter @engine/gameplay typecheck`
passes with the lockfile-pinned TypeScript 5.9.3.

**Honest cuts.** No live visual check: the new kinds have not been seen in the running game,
so Tracey's eyes on the live build are still the real check — especially the Watchtower
(2×2 tower beside a 3×3 hut), the Bathhouse fountain, and the Chapel pews. The stamp-timing
and bench numbers above are single-VM, noisy, and not a benchmark claim. Deliberately not
changed: loot tables, reclaim values, `SITE_CHANCE` beyond 0.15, the per-chunk one-site rule,
`ABANDONED_SCAN_RADIUS`, and anything in the stairs (ADR-372) or passenger (ADR-371) slices.

## ADR-374: Render warm-up actually pumps — first-view pages land before the first paint (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** Tracey reported the game is very slow and laggy on her phone since the
ADR-368–370 batch, especially at the beginning and when moving through new areas. The
performance investigation (PROFILE.md §2) proved ADR-370's warm-up window is structurally
stalled: `AtlasManager.beginFrame()` (`atlasManager.ts:1360`) is the only place that resets
`streamStarts` and `uploadsThisFrame`, and its only caller is `sprites.prepare()` — i.e. only
during a rendered frame. `warmupFirstView()` requested up to 24 pages at prio 1, then polled
for up to 1500 ms without ever calling `beginFrame()` or `pump()`; after 2 stream starts + 2
GPU uploads both gates stalled (`STREAM_UPLOADS_PER_FRAME = 2`, `PAGE_UPLOADS_PER_FRAME = 2`).
`iso` is only assigned after `IsoView.create` resolves (`main.ts:139`), so no frame renders
during the boot window. Expected result: resident ≈ alreadyResident + ~2, `timedOut: true`,
ms ≈ 1500 — boot ~1.5 s longer AND the first view still blurry, with the remaining ~20 pages
then landing at 2 uploads/frame during the first gameplay frames. Confirmed on Tracey's Galaxy
A16 (?diag=1, 2026-11-12, live build 07062533 — see PROFILE.md §8): boot warm-up 22/26 pages
resident in 1,506 ms (TIMED OUT, 4 pending), 9 pages still pending after the 1,628 ms
warmup-drain. The 22 resident were already resident before the poll (resident atlases / the
ADR-307 prefetch); the stalled poll itself added only ~2 — so this fix is judged on the
pending count going to ~0 inside the window, not on the resident count. The warm-up is only
~1.5 s of a 28.5 s boot; the rest of boot is a separate investigation (ADR-380), and this ADR
claims no boot-time fix. Two further defects in the
same path: `view.ts` called `warmupFirstView(warmupKeys)` with no opts (no `firstView`, no
`maxPages` — `warmupKeysForSprites()` unused at boot, so tier-0 ordering never happened), and
`warmupPageBudget()` existed but was never called (the 24-page cap was not clamped to the
12-slot low-memory stream pool).

**Decision — pump inside the wait loop (gap-fill tick).** New `AtlasManager.pumpWarmupTick()`:
the per-frame page-in budget reset that `beginFrame()` does, without a rendered frame. It
resets `streamStarts` / `uploadsThisFrame`, releases the next decoded pages waiting for their
upload turn (at most `PAGE_UPLOADS_PER_FRAME`), and re-drives `pump()`. Deliberately NOT
`beginFrame()`: it does not advance `this.frame` (the LRU clock, and the `unloadIdleStream`
cadence that runs off it — a warm-up tick can never evict a page), and it does no frame-table
GL upload (dirty rows upload on the first rendered frame's `beginFrame`). The tick itself
issues no GL calls; the only GL work it can trigger is `pageIn`'s own `texSubImage3D`
uploads — the same uploads a rendered frame performs, on the same context, which IsoRenderer
owns and which is current (`setRegistry` has run before the boot warm-up; no other GL user
runs during the boot window). The 2/frame caps are unchanged: the tick resets the same
counters `beginFrame` resets, to the same limits. `warmupFirstView()` calls the tick once per
poll (16 ms) **only when no rendered frame has run since the last poll** (tracked via
`this.frame`): at boot no frames exist, so every poll pumps; at world entry frames are
running, so `beginFrame` already pumps and the tick stays out of the way — at most one extra
pump per poll, each bounded by the same 2/frame caps, inside the same bounded 1500 ms window.
`warmupDrain()` is deliberately untouched: during the world-entry drain frames are running
(the rAF loop drives `iso.render` every frame), so it is already pumped, and adding a tick
there would only double-pump the same frames.

**Decision — clamp the request count to the real pool.** `warmupFirstView()` now computes its
cap as `warmupPageBudget(this.streamPoolSlots(), opts.maxPages ?? WARMUP_MAX_PAGES)` via the
new `streamPoolSlots()` (capacity of the main manifest stream-sheet pool: 24 desktop / 12
low-memory; the 2/1-slot oversize stream pool is not counted, so the clamp is conservative).
A 12-slot low-memory pool caps at 12 pages, not 24. The clamp lives inside
`warmupFirstView()` so it holds for every caller, and the boot call site in `view.ts` also
passes it explicitly (`{ maxPages: warmupPageBudget(renderer.atlas.streamPoolSlots?.()) }`).

**Decision — first-view set where it is knowable (world entry, not boot).** At boot no
first-view set is knowable — no world, player or camera target exists yet — so tier-0
ordering cannot happen there, and the boot call keeps the visible-pin set (now pool-clamped).
At world entry it is knowable: `main.ts` `drainFirstView()` now reads the sprite ids from
`iso.view` (the view world, synced by the frames that have already run — the rAF loop drives
`iso.render` from `useWorld` on, so by the time `waitForWorldReady` resolves the view holds
`Sprite` components for the entities actually around the player), turns them into page keys
with `warmupKeysForSprites()`, and calls `warmupFirstView(keys, { firstView: keys })` — those
pages sort tier 0 — before the existing `warmupDrain()`. A failure in that step is caught
and logged, never blocks `ready`: the drain still runs and the overlay still lifts on its own
timeout. Worst case the world-entry warm-up adds one more bounded 1500 ms wait before `ready`
(the same bound the drain already had); in practice it returns as soon as the pages land.
The result is recorded in the load-cost breakdown (`?diag=1`) alongside the drain note.

**Measurement — stubbed-manager regression test, not a browser.** Chrome is blocked in this
VM (it refuses localhost navigation), so there is no live frame-time measurement; the proof
is a gated fake manager in the new `packages/render/test/adr374_warmup_pump.test.ts` (5
tests), whose fake `request`/`pump` mirror the real gates (a page-in only starts while
`streamStarts < STREAM_UPLOADS_PER_FRAME`; only a pump tick resets it) with a 5 ms simulated
landing delay. Before / after on the same fake, 12 tier-1 pages, default 1500 ms window
(3 runs of a throwaway probe; the wall-clock ms is noisy on this loaded VM — the 16 ms polls
slip — the resident counts are stable):

| | requested | resident | stillPending | timedOut | ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before (tick stubbed = old wait loop) | 12 | 2 | 10 | true | 1507–1562 |
| After (fix) | 12 | 12 | 0 | false | 315 / 661 / 392 |

Judged on the pending count, as the phone data requires: before, 10 of the 12 requested pages
were still pending when the window expired (timedOut); after, 0 are pending and the window
returns early. The resident count is the wrong yardstick here — on the phone most pages were
already resident before the poll, so the fix's visible effect is pending → 0, not a higher
resident number.

The clamp on the same fake, 20 candidates: 12-slot pool → requested 12, skipped 8,
resident 12; 24-slot pool → requested 20, skipped 0; no stream pool → falls back to
`WARMUP_MAX_PAGES` (24); explicit `maxPages: 5` still wins (requested 5). The test file
fails on pre-fix code (4 of 5 fail: the landing test gets resident 2, the clamp test gets
requested 20, the tick unit test has no method to call, the frozen-frame test never ticks;
the fifth test encodes the old stall and passes on old code by design) and passes with the
fix (5/5). No graphics-quality change: no resolution / mip / preset / compass change, no
new art; the per-frame upload budgets are untouched for rendered frames.

**Validation.** New `packages/render/test/adr374_warmup_pump.test.ts` (5 tests, all pass).
Render suite: 75 files, 498 tests, all pass. Targeted client tests (`adr370_load_cost`,
`perf_budget`, both warm-up files): 4 files, 25 tests, all pass. `pnpm -r typecheck`
(lockfile-pinned TS 5.9.3): EXIT 0, all 11 projects. Client suite (`apps/client/test`):
174 files passed, 13 failed; 858 tests passed, 12 failed, 0 skipped — every failure
characterised in the ADR-374 report as pre-existing (9 art-file/count assertions + 3
ENOENT art-file unhandled errors on this sparse checkout, 2 timeouts reproduced identically
with the change stashed, 1 timing-sensitive UI test that passes standalone); none is caused
by this change. `warmupDrain()` unchanged, so the existing
ADR-370 drain test is unaffected; the ADR-370 fake manager keeps passing unmodified (its
`pools` field is absent, so `streamPoolSlots()` returns undefined and the budget falls back
to `WARMUP_MAX_PAGES`).

**Honest cuts.** No live visual check: the blurry start has not been seen fixed on Tracey's
phone — her eyes on the live build are still the real check, especially the first paint after
boot and the first seconds after entering a world, and the pending counts in `?diag=1` (boot
warm-up pending should go to ~0; warmup-drain pending should drop from 9). This ADR does NOT
fix the 28.5 s boot (ADR-380) or the in-game 15.7 ms frame CPU (ADR-381): the warm-up is
only ~1.5 s of the boot, and the in-game frame cost is a separate problem. The before/after
numbers above are from a
stubbed manager (fake decode + fake landing delay), not a GPU: real page-in cost per page
(fetch + `createImageBitmap` + upload) is device- and art-dependent, so 12 pages may still
take a visible fraction of the window on a slow phone — the window is bounded and the
timeout keeps boot soft either way. Not changed: `warmupDrain()`, the per-frame budgets,
`prefetch()` (same idle-poll shape, out of scope — it is only called from creator previews,
not boot), and anything in the sim / net / world-streaming slices.


## ADR-375: Net replicate — cut per-tick allocations (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** The performance investigation (PROFILE.md §3) measured `net.server.replicate` as the
single biggest system in the real-play harness (~5.3 ms/tick; send/encode ~2.5 ms/tick) with heavy
per-tick allocation that predates ADR-368/369: per client per tick a `view` Map, must/rest arrays,
and `prioritize()`'s Float64Array + order array + sorted score copy + head/tail arrays (+ a
concat copy), plus one `BitWriter` + `snapshotBits()` byte copy per encoded entity record. ADR-369's
dirty-driven capture is a real-play win and its relevant-netId cache is worth ~0 ms — neither is
touched here. The wire protocol stays v8; no format change, no replication-semantics change.

**What changed.** `packages/net/src/server.ts` (replicate + prioritize): must/rest/mustEs/restEs are
reused server-level scratch lists (length-reset per client); `prioritize()` works entirely on reused
scratch (score/sorted Float64Arrays, order/head/tail/cx/cy arrays) and returns the reused order buffer
— same scores, same stable sort, same threshold/head/tail partition including ties at the threshold;
the rest reorder permutes through reused scratch instead of `rest.slice()` / `restEs.slice()`; the
per-tick encoded-record cache keeps the `BitWriter` itself instead of a `snapshotBits()` byte copy
(the writer is written once and never mutated after, so `appendWriter()` reads it without copying);
the dead per-tick `globalSet` is removed and the per-client `ownedIds` Set is replaced by reading the
owned entities' netIds directly. `packages/net/src/bits.ts`: new `BitWriter.appendWriter()` (bit-identical
to appending a `snapshotBits()` copy) and `reset()` (zeroes used bytes first, because `writeBits` ORs).
`packages/net/src/state.ts`: `writeSpawnComp`'s sparse-vs-dense choice reuses two module-level scratch
writers instead of allocating two `BitWriter`s + a snapshot copy per wide-component spawn (synchronous,
never re-entrant, so sharing is safe). Deliberately not changed: `captureState` (ADR-376), the
relevant-netId cache, the per-client `view` Map (it is the stored delta baseline), the per-tick `enc`
and `chunkIds` maps, and the grid-sync viewpoint arrays.

**Behaviour — identical bytes on the wire.** New `packages/net/test/adr375_replicate_allocs.test.ts`
(5 tests): `appendWriter` matches `appendBits(snapshotBits())` at aligned and unaligned offsets;
`reset()` leaves no stale 1-bits; a scripted 2-client run (300 entities, `budgetBytes: 256`,
interest off, 40 ticks — exercises the prioritize limit path, the shared record cache and the order
tail) hashes byte-identically to the pre-375 baseline (SHA-256
`0e5064c6c59ecb774f362dc91f7e8770db138ded6809dd3f9b8cd59d64586222`); under a 64-byte budget the
nearest entity's spawn is sent on tick 1, the farthest is not, and the tail drains within 90 ticks
(no starvation). Full net suite: 41 files, 117/117 pass (including the 5 new tests and the copied probe).

**Measured — no speedup demonstrable, reported honestly.** The expected ~0.5–1.5 ms/tick did not
materialise in any measurement on this VM, so none is claimed. CPU-time bench (same scenarios as the
profiling worker's probe, timed with `process.cpuUsage()` over 120 ticks because wall time on this
1.5-CPU box is descheduling-dominated — wall was 4–10× CPU in the same runs): total CPU ms/tick,
medians of 3 runs, before → after: 1c×10k 10% moving 12.52 → 12.68, idle 7.08 → 7.14, 100% moving
23.81 → 22.95, 4c×10k 12.47 → 13.10, travelling 5 tiles/tick 11.59 → 12.16, 40 tiles/tick 11.38 →
12.10 — every delta inside the run-to-run ranges. GC in the same runs (median ms per 120 ticks):
342.7 → 386.8, 191.1 → 176.0, 615.5 → 642.4, 283.6 → 281.3, 287.6 → 295.3, 306.9 → 387.9 — also
flat, ranges overlapping widely. The wall-clock probe and real-play harness could not be compared at
all: the after-window ran under extreme VM contention (harness replicate 28.1 / 41.5 / 28.7 ms/tick
vs 6.5 before, with capture — untouched code — also 3–6× worse), so those after numbers measure the
neighbours, not this change. Why so little: in these scenarios the send path is a small share of the
tick (capture's O(N) fresh-Map allocation dominates) and the removed allocations are small in absolute
terms (tens of encodes and a small `rest` per client per tick). The allocation cut is real — zero
per-client-per-tick arrays in `prioritize()`, zero `slice()` copies, zero `snapshotBits()` copies per
record — but its payoff, if any, is in fewer GC pauses under real multi-client play, not in mean
ms/tick here; ADR-376 (captureState) is where the big allocation lives.

**Validation.** New `packages/net/test/adr375_replicate_allocs.test.ts`, 5/5 passing; full net suite
41 files, 117/117. `pnpm -r typecheck` passes with lockfile-pinned TypeScript 5.9.3.

**Honest cuts.** No live play check: whether this (or any of ADR-374–379) moves the lag Tracey feels
on her phone is still for her eyes on the live build — this slice on its own has no measurable
effect on this VM, and the harness numbers that would speak to real play were unusable under VM
contention. If the gate wants a sharper verdict, re-run the harness on a quiet machine (or with the
CPU-time method used here) rather than trusting the wall-clock after numbers in the slice REPORT.md.

## ADR-376: captureState O(N) floor — in-place WorldState, generation-stamped flags (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** The performance investigation (PROFILE.md §3) measured `captureState` at
~0.3 µs/entity/tick even at 0% dirty: the floor is an O(N) allocation problem, not a dirty
problem — a fresh ~N-entry `WorldState` Map every tick, plus two `Set.has` per entity
(`touched`, `dirty`), plus a `prev.get` per entity. ADR-369's dirty-driven capture is a real
win (real-play harness capture 2.02–2.48 vs pristine 2.74–3.29 ms/tick) and stays. This slice
cuts the floor underneath it, in `packages/net/src/state.ts` only. Wire protocol stays v8.

**Decision — update the WorldState Map in place.** `captureState` now returns `prev` itself,
mutated, instead of a fresh Map: clean entities are skipped with no `Map.get` and no
`Map.set` (their entry already sits in the map with its previous immutable `EntityState`);
changed entities are rebuilt exactly as before and `out.set` in place. **Contract change:**
callers must NOT retain `prev` as a snapshot — copy it (`new Map(prev)`) first if the old
contents are needed. The only production caller is `NetServer.replicate`, which only ever
passes its own `prevState` straight into the next capture; per-client `base` maps are the
separate per-tick `view` maps (fresh each tick, holding `EntityState` refs), `StaticServer`
keeps its own chunk maps, and the client's `history` maps come from `decodeDelta` — none of
them alias the captured map, so none of them is affected. `EntityState` objects stay
immutable and structurally shared exactly as before. A non-`Map` `ReadonlyMap` passed as
`prev` is copied, not mutated (`prev instanceof Map` guard).

**Decision — generation-stamped Uint16Arrays instead of Sets.** Two module-level
`Uint16Array(1 << 20)` (`dirtyMarks`, `touchedMarks`, indexed by entity index — always
< 2^20 by core's `INDEX_MASK`, so no growth and no bounds check) plus a 16-bit generation
bumped per call replace the `touched`/`dirty` Sets: a stamp write on mark, a typed-array
read on test, no hashing. Wrap (fill + restart) is a once-per-65535-calls event. Stamps are
written and read inside a single call, so sharing them across worlds/servers is safe.
`captureState` is not re-entrant.

**Decision — the leave scan.** Entities that left are dropped by a key scan over the map,
but only when needed: the scan runs only if `out.size > live`, where `live` counts distinct
live netIds stamped this tick (a third stamp array, `seenMarks`, indexed by netId, doubling
to the largest netId ever assigned — the same growth the server's own netId-indexed
`curArr`/`stamp` already do). No-leave ticks skip the scan entirely. `live` is a distinct
count, not `ns.size`, because two live entities can share a netId in hand-built worlds
(the world's environment singleton already holds netId 1) — using `ns.size` would skip the
scan and resurrect a stale entry, which the ADR-376 tests pin. A first capture (`prev`
undefined) rebuilds everything, as before, even if the change bits were already cleared.

**Tests updated for the contract change.** Three existing files held a `prev` snapshot and
used it as an `encodeDelta` base or a `.toBe` reference after the next capture; they now
take a `new Map(prev)` copy (or hold the `EntityState` ref) before capturing:
`packages/net/test/delta.test.ts`, `packages/net/test/adr369_net_replication.test.ts`
(its `.toBe(s0…)` comparisons now use a pre-capture copy), and
`apps/server/test/container_bandwidth.test.ts`. No assertion was weakened — the same stats,
the same decoded-state equality, the same byte-size bounds.

**Verification.** New `packages/net/test/adr376_capture_floor.test.ts` (6 tests): the
returned map `toBe`s `prev` and an idle tick changes nothing; a first capture with no prev
still captures everything after `clearChanges`; destroy + NetId-removal drops the entries,
`encodeDelta` against a pre-capture copy reports exactly those despawns, later ticks do not
resurrect them, and a newcomer joins cleanly; leave + same-netId re-add in one tick
reflects the new entity; a 100-entity mass leave keeps the 50 survivors' exact
`EntityState` objects under churn with index reuse; a scripted change sequence produces
deterministic, decodable delta bytes. Full net suite: 42 files, 118 tests, all pass
(includes the 6 new tests and the probe's 3). `pnpm -r typecheck` EXIT 0 with the
lockfile-pinned TypeScript 5.9.3.

**Measurement — the floor is cut ~4.5×; the dirty path is within noise on this VM.**
`captureState`-alone micro-probe (profiling worker's probe, 1k/5k/10k × 0%/10%/100% dirty,
40 samples each, median of run-medians; baseline 3 runs, after 6 runs, same VM):

| entities | 0% dirty before → after | 10% dirty before → after | 100% dirty before → after |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1k | 0.124 → 0.045 ms | 0.229 → 0.131 ms | 0.547 → 0.579 ms |
| 5k | 0.872 → 0.221 ms | 1.446 → 0.677 ms | 3.200 → 5.43 ms |
| 10k | 1.941 → 0.421 ms | 3.421 → 3.29 ms | 7.541 → 55.08 ms |

The 0%-dirty floor is the clean win: 0.19 → 0.042 µs/entity/tick, ranges
non-overlapping at 5k/10k (10k: before 1.913–2.261, after 0.412–0.467 ms). At harness
scale (~3,692 entities) that floor saving is ~(0.19 − 0.04) µs × 3,692 ≈ 0.55 ms/tick
— arithmetic from the micro-probe, not a harness measurement (see below). The 10% and
100% medians are NOT usable as a before/after claim on this VM: other agents were running
full vitest suites concurrently on the shared 1.5-CPU box, and the after-runs' dirty-path
p90s run 60–196 ms (VM descheduling + GC pauses; PROFILE.md already proved maxima
> ~15 ms are descheduling, wall 51 ms vs CPU 2 ms on identical work). The p10s — the
least-contended samples — show the dirty path roughly flat to ~20% better (10k 100%:
before p10 median 7.04 ms, after 7.7 ms across 6 runs; 10k 10%: 3.13 → 1.23 ms), so no
dirty-path regression is visible, but no dirty-path speedup is claimed either. The
expected 0.3–0.8 ms/tick in the brief is the floor saving above; the dirty path was
never the floor.

**Measurement — real-play harness A/B is inconclusive (VM contention, not the change).**
`apps/client/perf/run.ts --seconds 15` (300 ticks, 3,692 entities): baseline capture
4.51 / 9.59 / 8.10 ms/tick (median 8.10), totals 40.3 / 50.5 / 46.6; after capture
10.67–18.37 (median 12.8 then 15.3 over 6 runs), totals 96.7–129.7. The whole harness
got ~2.3× slower, including code this slice never touches (`send/encode` 6.7–8.6 →
15.9–23.6 ms/tick) while up to 28 foreign vitest workers were running — so the harness
cannot separate this change from contention, and no harness number is claimed either
way. Heap Δ shows no consistent difference (baseline 6.3 / 27.2 / 31.8 MB; after 1.3 /
20.7 / 34.3 / 56.7 / −19.9 / 101.6 MB across 6 runs) — the one-Map-per-tick saving is
swamped by everything else the harness allocates.

**Wire identity — snapshot bytes identical to two decimals in all 8 probe scenarios.**
The probe's `bytesPerClientTick` totals moved by 1 in two scenarios (201 → 202,
228 → 229), which looked like a wire change until the transport bytes were split by
message type (header byte 2: Snapshot = 5, Ping = 15): the entire difference is
wall-clock `NetServer.pings()` — one 9-byte Ping per 1000 ms of wall time, counted by the
probe's transport. Snapshot-only bytes/client/tick, pristine vs after: 201.45 / 201.45,
32.75 / 32.75, 642.03 / 642.03, 48.57 / 48.57, 137.07 / 137.07, 182.28 / 182.28,
210.30 / 210.30, 228.45 / 228.45. `encodesPerTick` is identical in every scenario
(21 / 2 / 71 / 4 / 14 / 75 / 21 / 22). Protocol stays v8; no format change.

**Honest cuts.** No live-phone check: the numbers above are all from this VM, and the
harness A/B that would show the saving in real play is inconclusive for contention
reasons — Tracey's eyes on her phone are still the real check, and the saving only
shows up as ~0.5 ms/tick of a ~15 ms/tick budget, so it is a floor cut, not a fix for
the lag by itself. The 4 MB of stamp arrays (2 × 1M × 2 bytes) is static, allocated
lazily on first capture. Deliberately not changed: `prioritize()`/send (ADR-375's
worker), the per-client relevant cache, the per-entity rebuild path, the wire format,
and the fully-idle-tick skip (the harness is never fully idle, and the floor cut already
covers it — skipping capture on fully-idle ticks would only help truly idle worlds).

## ADR-377: animalAI — cache the animal lists, square the distances (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** Profiling (PROFILE.md §3) put `gameplay.animalAI` at ~2.2 ms/tick in the
real-play harness — the #1 sim cost — and ~2.6 µs/animal/tick open-ground, ~5 µs in a walled
base. Two suspects: the system spread + sorted the animal query every tick (a fresh array
for the dead sweep, `[...query].sort(...)`, plus a fresh array for the live list,
`[...world.query([Animal, Transform], [Dead, Pet])]`), and `Math.hypot` everywhere a
comparison would do. No gameplay or balance change was wanted: animals must behave
identically, just cheaper.

**Decision — cache both lists, keyed on `ComponentStore.membership`.** `animalAISystem`
(`packages/gameplay/src/population.ts`) now keeps a per-world (WeakMap) cache of the dead
list (ascending by entity id, exactly as the old sort produced) and the live list (rebuilt
with the same query expression, so its order — reverse-dense of the Animal store, the query
driver — is identical). A list rebuilds only when a membership counter of a store that
gates its membership moves: Animal/Dead for the dead list, Animal/Transform/Dead/Pet for
the live list. `membership` bumps on add/remove and never on field writes (the ADR-315
precedent), and it only ever increases, so a spawn and a destroy in the same tick still
invalidate (net-zero churn cannot hide). The live list is re-validated after the dead
sweep, because the sweep's corpse destroys and loot-bag Transform adds move the counters.
Field writes by this system itself (state/thinkAt/goal) never invalidate. Dead animals,
new spawns, and mid-run pets all invalidate through the same counters (a pet gains Pet,
a corpse gains Dead, a spawn adds Animal).

**Decision — squared distances where only ordering/comparison matters.** `homeD`,
threat `d`, retaliation `d` and territory `d` are now squared distances (`d2`), compared
against squared thresholds (leash, aggro range, flee range, attack range + 0.4, press-home).
The nearest-threat tie-break (`d2 === threat.d2 && p < threat.e`) keeps the lower entity
id on ties, as before. The one true distance is kept: movement still uses
`Math.hypot(dx, dy)` for normalisation and `Math.min(sp, d)`. `nearestClaimHostile`
