(still `Math.hypot` inside) is untouched — it runs only for tame defenders with a tribe.
No tuning values changed; nothing in `packages/gameplay/data/*.json` was touched.

**Deliberately not done — threat-evaluation staggering.** The code has no think-gate for
threat scanning: `thinkAt` gates attack cooldowns and wander re-rolls only. Gating the
scan on `thinkAt` would delay flee/engage by up to the think interval — a behaviour
change, not a pure optimisation — so the scan still runs every tick for every live animal.

**Behaviour identity — proven, not asserted.** New
`packages/gameplay/test/adr377_animal_ai.test.ts` (7 tests) pins the exact decisions of
a deterministic 800-tick world (160 animals + 16 pets + 20 zombies + 4 walking players,
open ground and walled base): every live animal's id/kind/state/position/goal/thinkAt/hp,
every loot bag's id/position, and the entity count, hashed. Golden hashes are identical
before and after the fix (open `64878346`, base `6402418b`), and identical again in the
direct-call micro-bench scenario (open `12102476`, base `db95b565`, 2,200 calls each).
Targeted tests cover the cache transitions directly: dead-sweep loot drops in ascending
animal-id order; a wolf spawned mid-run attacks on its first tick; destroying an animal
mid-run neither crashes nor stalls the others; a pet made mid-run leaves the live list
(its wander goal freezes); the nearest-threat tie breaks to the lower entity id. The
squared-distance boundary risk is a rounding one only: `d <= R` vs `d2 <= R²` can differ
by an ulp at an exact boundary, and the golden hashes (which cover thousands of
comparisons) show no flip.

**Measured — honest numbers, and where they are weak.** All numbers on this VM (shared
1.5-CPU box) while six investigation workers measured at the same time; absolute ms are
NOT phone ms and the full-sim probes were contention-polluted — load averages 4–14
during the runs, and every system inflated together (e.g. `zombieAI` base x3 went
2.07 → 8.3 ms/tick between windows with no code change). The controlled result is an
interleaved micro-benchmark (direct `animalAISystem` calls, 2,000 calls, same 160-animal
worlds, fix/baseline alternating within minutes): open ground fixed 1.85 ms/call
(median of 3: 1.85, 2.34, 1.66) vs baseline 3.76 (3.04, 3.84, 3.76) — about 1.9 ms/call
saved, non-overlapping ranges, most of it the per-tick spread/sort allocation and the
dead-sweep generator scan, not just the `hypot`s. Walled base was inconclusive there
(fixed 9.25 [5.05–9.41] vs baseline 6.90 [6.24–12.45] — overlapping ranges, and the
micro-bench teleports players through walls so animals pathfind constantly, 5–12 ms/call
vs the probe's 1.4–1.8, a pathological scenario). The sim-breakdown probe, bench215 and
the real-play harness could not resolve the effect in this window: breakdown baselines
(open x1 0.82, base x1 1.64, open x3 0.77, base x3 3.82 ms/tick) vs after-runs under heavy
load (2.65, 8.99, 8.84, 22.80) are not comparable; bench215 after-runs 2–3 timed out
(>300 s test timeout) under load (baseline open 1.27, base 3.77); harness animalAI
baseline 5.89 ms/tick median (already 2.7× PROFILE.md's 2.17 — heavy load) vs after
19.69, with a contemporaneous baseline of 13.82 in the same saturated window as the load
fell — overlapping ranges, no conclusion. The expected ~0.5–1 ms/tick is therefore NOT
claimed for real play: the fix is measurably cheaper per call on open ground, provably
behaviour-identical, and shows no slowdown anywhere it could be measured. The real-play
number needs a quiet box or Tracey's phone.

**Validation.** Neighbouring suites pass with the fix: animals / population / pets /
task14 / task15 / task32 / adr353 / adr319 / adr377 / adr368 — 10 files, 122 tests, all
passing. `pnpm -r typecheck` with the lockfile-pinned TypeScript 5.9.3: EXIT 0, all
projects. The full gameplay suite could not complete in this window: the run was
starved by concurrent sibling workers (11 s of CPU in 17 min of wall time) and was
killed; the gate must run it on a quieter box before any push.

## ADR-379: Chunk-load budget enforcement — make `maxLoadTimeMs` real (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** The profiling worker (PROFILE.md §4) found the chunk-load budget absent in
practice: `maxLoadTimeMs = 2` was checked only *between* chunks and the first chunk was
always admitted, so a 4-chunk update cost ≥2.8 ms of terrain gen alone and a single median
site chunk (4.3 ms) blew the budget 2× by itself; 22–23 of 23–24 boot updates and 10–11 of
11 teleport-burst updates exceeded 2 ms. `maxLoadsPerUpdate = 4` was the only effective cap.
The FIFO drain itself was fine (no starvation, queue keeps up at vehicle speed) — purely
the time budget was not enforced. Tracey's symptom this addresses: laggy all the time,
worse at boot and when moving through new areas while a lot loads at once.

**Decision — enforce the budget after every install, and predict before the next chunk.**
In `packages/world/src/chunkManager.ts` `update()`, the load loop now (a) checks elapsed
wall time *after* every chunk install and stops when it reaches `maxLoadTimeMs`, and (b)
before starting the next chunk, stops when elapsed + the cost of the chunk just loaded
would exceed the budget. Load cost is `provider.load` + `install`, so the `onLoad` stamp
(`apps/server/src/game.ts`: abandoned sites) counts against the budget. A chunk that
starts always finishes — the budget never aborts the current chunk, only further chunks
in that update — so there is no half-installed chunk and no starvation: the first chunk
of an update is always admitted. No change to load radius, cache size, unload margin, or
FIFO order (the ADR-370 nearest-first revert stays reverted — it starved far chunks and
broke ADR-252 bots). `maxLoadsPerUpdate` stays 4 in `game.ts` as the hard cap for cheap
chunks; the time budget governs. The knobs are not data-driven (single hardcoded call
site in `game.ts:187`), so the tuning stays there with an ADR-379 comment; no data file
owns them.

**Why no separate "cap at 2 after a site chunk" rule.** The task's first prescription
was to lower `maxLoadsPerUpdate` to 2 when a site chunk was just loaded; its alternative
was to account stamp cost in the budget so a site chunk consumes the budget it used. This
ADR takes the alternative, because with a time budget configured the cap rule is
unobservable — a site chunk's own cost (≥ the budget) already ends its update via the
after-install check — and without a budget a "site chunk" could only be guessed from cost,
which misfires on JIT-warm-up chunks (proved while implementing: the guess capped the
`streaming.test.ts` "respects per-update load budget" case at 2 loads on a slow first
chunk). The stamp-cost accounting is what makes the rule unnecessary, and it composes
with time-sliced stamping (ADR-378, reverted from this batch pending a redesign — see
that ADR's follow-up) without either side knowing about the other: a sliced stamp costs
less per tick, so more chunks fit that tick's budget.

**Performance.** Recreated the profiling worker's scenarios as a temporary vitest bench
against the real server wiring (`ChunkManager` + `ProceduralGenerator` + the `game.ts`
`onLoad` hook with resource nodes + `stampAbandonedChunk`), 3 seeds × 3 runs each, before
vs after. Plain-chunk updates (no site stamped) — the thing this ADR can fix:

| scenario | over-2 ms fraction (wall) before → after | median (wall) before → after |
|---|---|---|
| S5 boot drain (52 chunks) | 98% → 44% | 2.5 ms → 2.0 ms |
| S4 vehicle speed (200 updates) | 64% → 35% | 2.3 ms → 1.6 ms |
| S6 teleport burst (25 chunks) | 95% → 37% | 2.7 ms → 1.8 ms |

Loads/update moved from {1: 73, 2: 82, 3: 77} to {1: 228, 2: 117, 3: 2} on boot — the
3-chunk update is essentially gone (the two remaining 3-load updates are cheap-chunk
updates that fit the budget, which is correct behaviour). Boot drain takes more updates
(median 24 → 35) and still completes every time (52/52 chunks, pending 0); the vehicle
queue still keeps up (maxPending 4, same as before). CPU-time medians agree with the
wall-clock direction (plain-only CPU median 3.0 → 1.9 ms on boot). No speedup is claimed
for total chunk work — the same chunks load, spread over more updates; that is the point.

**Honest cuts.** Plain-chunk updates do not reach ~0% over budget: 35–44% still exceed
2 ms on wall clock. The residual is single-chunk cost, which no between-chunk budget can
remove: a 1-load update over 2 ms is one slow chunk (first-chunk JIT warm-up, GC, or VM
descheduling — wall p95 runs 60–100 ms on this shared-CPU VM while CPU medians sit near
2 ms), and the prediction uses the last chunk's cost, so per-chunk variance (0.7–1.3 ms)
can push a predicted-1.6 ms 2-chunk update to ~2.2 ms. Updates containing a site chunk
are still ~93–100% over 2 ms (median ~10 ms CPU) — a site chunk alone is 4–9 ms, so no
chunk-count rule can fix it; that is the job of time-sliced stamping (ADR-378, reverted
from this batch pending a redesign), and this ADR's accounting is what will let a sliced
stamp share the budget instead of blowing it. The
numbers are VM-noisy (after-runs ran under heavier contention than before-runs); the
loads/update distribution and the fake-clock regression tests are the deterministic
evidence, the ms are the direction. No live phone check: Tracey's eyes are still the
real check for boot and new-area hitches.

**Tests changed deliberately, and one server-suite finding.** The budget spreads
loading over more ticks, so a test that asserts on streamed content after a
fixed tick count is now wrong by design: `apps/server/test/craft_queue.test.ts`
(pre-81a7b11 save) asserted restored pieces after `tick(5)`, and failed under
parallel load (0 pieces — the pieces' chunks had not streamed yet) while passing
standalone; it now ticks until `chunks.pendingLoads` drains before asserting,
which is what the test means (save-load correctness, not streaming speed). The
same 9-file set passes 27/27 with that change. The remaining server-suite
failures seen during validation are 5 s timeouts in save/load + network tests
that also fail on the pristine copy under the same parallel load (4/27 there),
i.e. pre-existing contention flakiness on this shared-CPU VM, not a regression
from this patch — verified by an A/B with the budget disabled (27/27 pass) and
by the standalone passes. The ADR-252 bot live test (`adr252_ai_humans_live`,
8 tests) passes: the FIFO order the bots depend on is untouched.

## ADR-380: Boot time — split the boot bucket, then cut the dominant cost (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** Tracey's Galaxy A16 (`?diag=1`, 2026-11-12) shows boot = 28,506 ms (84% of the 34,041 ms total load). The ADR-370 warm-up explains only 1,506 ms of it, so ~27 s is elsewhere — but `boot` was recorded as ONE bucket (`main.ts:124` → `IsoView.create` resolving), so the split between renderer init, manifest, runtime-painted atlases, `setRegistry` (fetch + decode + rescale + upload + sprite tables), warm-up, variants and lighting was unknown from code alone. Inside `setRegistry` → `rebuild()` the candidates, in likely order: fetch + decode of the resident atlas set (a `Promise.all` over all atlases, colour + emissive + up to 3 masks, `fitToPage` resizes, KTX2→ASTC transcode); `fitBudget` / `halveSide` image rescales (the ADR-220 comment says they "take seconds"); `upload()` of 19 layers @2048 px with full mip chains (~187 MB through `texImage2D` on a Mali GPU); the sprite runtime-table loop (`list.find` per sprite, O(S×A): 5,326 sprites × ~654 atlases); body page-ins; runtime-painted atlases and the ~1 MB pack manifest parse. The ADR-307 prefetch warms Cache Storage in parallel with the bundle, so network fetches may already be cache hits — decode + rescale + upload are the costs it cannot hide.

**Decision — split the boot bucket into sub-phases in `?diag=1`.** `LoadCostBreakdown.recordSub(stage, name, ms)` (load-progress.ts, pure) records a sub-phase inside an already-recorded phase; sub-phases are a split of the parent, never added to the total, and render as `boot 28506ms (84%) [renderer 120ms · manifest 340ms · registry.fetch 9200ms · ...] · total 34041ms`. `IsoView.create` times each step (renderer / manifest / painted / registry.* / warmup / variants / lighting) and stores them on the view (`view.bootPhases`); `AtlasManager.rebuildTimings` times the rebuild phases (fetchDecode / fitBudget / halveSide / layout / upload / tables / bodies / restore) and `IsoView.create` folds them in as `registry.*` sub-phases (a single `registry` phase when the timings are unavailable, e.g. the Canvas2D renderer). `main.ts` records the sub-phases after `boot` and adds an `other` remainder (boot total minus the timed phases: module start, BootUI, menu setup) when it is positive. The instrumentation is a handful of `performance.now()` marks at boot only — no per-frame cost, no allocations in the render loop.

**Decision — sprite runtime tables: Map lookups, byte-identical.** The rebuild-time table build is extracted to exported pure `buildSpriteTables(registry, list)` (atlasManager.ts): two id→atlas/index Maps built once replace `list.find` / `list.findIndex` / `list.indexOf` per sprite. The output is byte-identical — the same atlas object and index per sprite, and -1 for a missing dirFrames page (`list[-1]` is undefined, so `dirFrameIndex` falls back to `d.frame` exactly as before) — proven by a test that builds both the old loop (copied verbatim) and the new function on the real merged manifest (762 atlases, 4,947 sprites, 348,144 dirFrames entries) and deep-equals them. `frameTintRows` gets the same treatment (one Map per call instead of `list.find` per tinted sprite) and is now computed once per rebuild and reused for the OOM re-uploads instead of once per upload call. Measured on this VM (shared 1.5-CPU box, medians of 7 runs each, interleaved, three separate runs): old loop 6,908–9,517 ms → new loop 981–1,688 ms — 5.6–8.4×. Absolute ms are VM ms, not phone ms; the phone saving is unknown until the new `?diag=1` split lands, but the ratio is the evidence. A probe of the new loop shows the remaining ~1.0–1.7 s (VM) is allocation-bound, not lookup-bound: Map lookups alone are 169 ms; the rest is `Int32Array.from` per dirFrames entry (348,144 entries), per-sprite `Int16Array` state anims, and object allocation — a flat-typed-array redesign would be needed to cut it further, and is deliberately not in this slice.

**Decision — resize slicing off during the initial `setRegistry`.** The ADR-190 resizer (`resizeImage` → `sliced()`) yields one frame per 6 ms of resize work so a mid-game re-tier cannot freeze a frame — but during boot there are no frames to protect, and the yield turns resize CPU into wall time at ~2.7× (one ~16 ms frame per 6 ms slice at 60 fps). Every boot resize goes through it: `fitToPage` in the load phase, `fitBudget`'s downscales, `halveSide`. New `setResizeSlicing(on)` (atlasManager.ts, exported via `@engine/render`) disables the yield; `IsoView.create` turns it off around the initial `setRegistry` only (restored in `finally`) — re-tiers keep slicing. The loading bar does not lose information from this: no new progress arrives during the rescale steps (the bar's target is set by fetch completions, which happen before), it just stops easing for the burst instead of easing while boot stretches. Proven by test, not by phone ms: with a fake clock/yield, 120 jobs × 3 ms complete with 0 frame yields while slicing is off (360 ms of work in one frame's worth of wall time) versus ~60 yields with slicing on; re-enabling restores the ≤6 ms (+1 job) per-frame cap.

**Not changed.** Full stays the default preset and full-resolution rendering; no resolution, mip-level, texture-quality, bloom or lighting change; compass untouched; no new art, recolors, or binary art; no gameplay, balance, or tuning values; the warm-up window is untouched (ADR-374 owns it); chunk loading is untouched (ADRs 378/379 own it); re-tier slicing, `RESIZE_SLICE_MS`, and the resize memoization are untouched; `BOOT_STAGES` weights and the loading bar are untouched.

**Validation.** New `packages/render/test/adr380_boot.test.ts` (2 tests): real-registry table equality + timing (above) and the slicer on/off/yield-restore test. New `apps/client/test/adr380_boot_load_cost.test.ts` (4 tests): sub-phase formatting, total unchanged by subs, unknown-stage/invalid-sub handling, subs coexisting with notes; the ADR-370 format output is unchanged when there are no subs. `pnpm --filter @engine/render typecheck` and `pnpm --filter @engine/client typecheck` pass with lockfile-pinned TypeScript 5.9.3 (the render typecheck initially failed: `AtlasRT` was not exported while the new public `buildSpriteTables` names it — `AtlasRT` and `SpriteRT` are now exported). Neighbouring suites run in this slice: render `retier_sliced`, `adr370_warmup`, `dirframes`, `frametable_rows` and client `load_progress`, `adr370_load_cost` — all pass; the full gate runs the rest.

**Honest cuts.** No live browser measurement was possible in this VM (Chrome refuses localhost navigation), so no phone ms are claimed for any cut: the tables saving is a VM ratio, the slicer saving is a mechanism proof (yields 60 → 0 for 360 ms of resize work), and the fetch/decode and upload phases are still unmeasured headlessly — the new `?diag=1` boot split is the instrument that measures them, on Tracey's phone, after this ships. The 28.5 s boot is therefore NOT claimed fixed by this slice: the tables cut is real but small against 28.5 s, and the slicer cut's phone size is unknown until the split lands. What still needs Tracey's eyes: a fresh `?diag=1` screenshot after this lands, reading the new boot sub-phase bracket — whichever sub-phase still dominates is the next cut. If `registry.upload` dominates, the fix is a GL-side change (upload batching / fewer mip levels) that cannot be validated headlessly and needs its own slice; if `registry.fetch` dominates, the fix is in decode (KTX2 for resident atlases needs build-time transcoding, also its own slice).

## ADR-381: In-game frame CPU — per-phase timings, cutaway cache, static piece cache (SurVivaZ)

**Apply order note.** This entry is appended after the ADR-373 tail in the patch, but in
apply order it follows ADR-380 (boot): the gate agent applies 374, then 375, 376, 377, 378,
379, 380, then 381, and this entry lands after ADR-380's entry. Expected tail text after
all eight apply: `... ADR-380 ...` followed by this `## ADR-381: In-game frame CPU` entry.
This patch's `docs/DECISIONS.md` hunk anchors on the ADR-373 entry, the last in the base —
the same convention as the 371/372/373 patches, which all anchored on ADR-370 and were
resolved by applying in order at gate time.

**Context.** Tracey's Galaxy A16 (Mali-G68) reports an in-game frame of 15.7 ms CPU at only
22 draws / 228 sprites with 1,056 entities in view (`?diag=1`). Frame cpu is
`IsoRenderer.render()` wall time — JS CPU for the whole render call, so 22 draws cannot cost
15.7 ms: it is render-PREP, not draw calls, and the same thread also runs sim (~9.8 ms/tick)
and net replicate (~5.3 ms/tick), so a real frame is far over the 16.7 ms budget. The game is
not GPU-bound and not VRAM-bound (186.7/256 MB, 0 evictions) — it is JS-CPU-bound on the
render thread. Code-reading found the suspects, and a headless bench
(`packages/render/test/adr381_prepare_bench.test.ts`, stub atlas + stub GL, 1,200 sprites +
800 pieces) confirmed the shape before any fix: `gatherPieces` dominates (~9.6 ms for 800
pieces vs ~2.6 ms for the 1,200-sprite loop), an active indoor cutaway roughly doubles the
cost, and the per-frame cutaway BFS itself costs ~1.35 ms/call (gridless `PieceCoverIndex.region`)
while the grid path (`cutawayRegion`, demo/test-only in production) costs ~6.17 ms/call.
`seasonPick` and the focus setup are NOT measurable culprits (ablations within noise).
Two PROFILE.md suspects turned out wrong for the real client: the client never calls
`setSpatialIndex` (only the render demo does), so the `cx.spatial` branch in `prepare()` is
dead in production, and it never calls `setBuildingGrid`, so the grid `cutawayRegion` path
does not run in production — the production cutaway is the gridless `PieceCoverIndex.region`.
`updateBuildingTiers` runs every 15th frame, not per frame, and the `Array.from(...).sort(...)`
in `sprites.ts` runs only on static-chunk rebuild, not per draw.

**What changed.**
1. **Per-phase timings (instrumentation).** `packages/render/src/gl/util.ts` gains
`RenderPhaseMs` (prep / sprites / upload / lightsPrep / scene / light / bloom / composite /
weather), `newPhaseMs()`, and a `PhaseTimer` class (one reused record, no per-frame
allocation; callers pass `performance.now()` readings, so it is unit-testable with synthetic
timestamps; `zero(name)` marks a phase that did not run without advancing the clock).
`IsoRenderer.render()` splits the timer around each phase and stores the last frame's
values on `stats.phases` next to `stats.cpuMs`; `apps/client/src/diag.ts` shows them in the
`?diag=1` overlay as a `phases prep … spr … upl … lit … scn … lgt … blm … cmp … wth …` line,
so the split is measurable on Tracey's phone after this ships.
2. **Cutaway cache.** `prepare()` recomputes the cutaway region only when its inputs change
— the player tile/level, the `PieceCoverIndex` fingerprint + size (gridless path), or
`BuildingGrid.version` (grid path); otherwise the cached `Set<number>` is returned (callers
only `.has()` it, read-only, so sharing is safe). A standing-still player indoors used to
pay the flood-fill every frame. `PieceCoverIndex` gains a rolling 32-bit fingerprint
(bumped per `add()`, reset in `clear()`); both `region()` and the grid `cutawayRegion` now
use packed numeric tile keys (`tileKey`, `(x + 32768) * 65536 + (y + 32768)`, the same bound
as the existing chunk keys) and an index queue instead of `q.shift()` and per-tile string
keys. `footprintHits` / `gatherPieces` take `Set<number>`.
3. **Per-part static piece cache.** `gatherPieces` used to rebuild every static piece's
instances every frame — per-column slice loop, crack block, and a per-frame FNV hash over
every static piece's floats — then rebuild every static chunk's GPU buffer whenever the
chunk checksum moved. Now each part (a piece has up to 3: 2 L-corner arms + post) is cached
under a 32-field signature covering every input to its instances (visual/variant/rotation/
level/layer/ghost/damage/tint/season/resolved frame/deck/crack/view quarter/layout version/
entity index/night/piece anchor); static means not dynamic, so cutaway/alpha/occlusion/
animated need no fields (static pieces have cutaway=false, alpha=1, occT=0, animated=false)
and fire>0 pieces are never cached. On a hit, the slice loop, crack block and FNV hash are
skipped; the chunk sum is the XOR of its parts' per-part hashes ^ total float count
(order-independent, so dense reordering alone does not rebuild); the instance list is
rebuilt from cache entries only for changed chunks, and unchanged chunks keep their GPU
buffer. The ADR-328 keep-alive (a chunk whose pieces are all dynamic this frame stays
alive but empty so its fade-in clock survives) is preserved, now driven by the per-frame
dynamic-part count. One intentional behaviour difference: a chunk whose pieces are all
hidden while off screen used to have its static buffer deleted via its stale empty scratch
entry and rebuilt on return; it is now kept by the off-screen sweep (the sum comparison
still rebuilds it if any piece changed while hidden) — correct, and one fewer rebuild.
4. **Alloc removals in the same loop.** `AtlasManager.pieceInfo` (fresh `{fw,fh,layer}` per
call, twice per piece per frame) is cached per atlas layout version; `viewRect` is inlined
in `gatherPieces` (it allocated a fresh `{x,y,w,h}` per piece per frame); the common
single-part case reuses one scratch part object instead of `parts.push({...})` per piece.
The per-frame `pieceChecks` checksum map is gone (replaced by the per-part hashes).

**Performance.** Headless bench `packages/render/test/adr381_prepare_bench.test.ts`
(PERF=1, stub atlas + stub GL, 1,200 sprites + 800 pieces, medians of 7 runs × 500 frames
of `SpriteBatch.prepare()`), run twice patched and twice on pristine
(`~/workspace/SurVivaZ-perf`, 0706253) on the same shared 1.5-CPU VM. The box itself
swings hard between runs (sprites-only, a path this patch does not touch, measured 2.57,
1.01, 3.08 and 0.95 ms across the four runs — a 3x swing), so no single ms figure is
claimable; only same-evening paired comparisons are. Pair A (pristine vs patched ~15 min
apart): pieces-only 9.17 → 7.77, mixed outdoor 12.81 → 11.54, mixed indoor 20.80 → 11.38.
Pair B (pristine vs patched minutes apart): pieces-only 5.13 → 2.40, mixed outdoor
6.45 → 3.56, mixed indoor 6.39 → 5.22. Control scenario sprites-only is flat in both
pairs (2.57 → 3.08, 1.01 → 0.95), as expected. Read conservatively: `prepare()` is
~1.2–2x faster on piece-heavy scenes, with the indoor gain the most consistent; the
bimodal slow cluster the unpatched indoor runs showed (25–28 ms, likely GC churn from
the per-frame allocations this patch removes) never appears in either patched run (tight
9.4–13.5 and 4.6–6.4). The direct flood-fill numbers are NOT claimable: `cover.region`
measured 0.29 / 0.51 pristine vs 0.61 / 0.39 patched and `cutawayRegion` 1.02 / 3.54 vs
6.00 / 2.06 across the same runs, and a standalone 4-variant diagnostic scored the
pristine-style string+shift loop slowest and the patched key-once loop fastest — the
reverse of the first isolated comparison. One robust lesson survived the diagnostic:
computing the tile key once per neighbour beats twice (1.49 vs 2.76 ms/call), so
`cutawayRegion` hoists it. No phone ms are claimed; the stub resolve understates the
production `resolvePiece` cost, so the bench over-weights the cached slice/hash work.

**Validation.** New `packages/render/test/adr381_phases.test.ts` (5 tests, run in normal CI):
PhaseTimer splits with synthetic timestamps (incl. `zero()` not advancing the clock);
`PieceCoverIndex.region` numeric keys + fingerprint change/reset; `prepare()` twice on an
unchanged world produces identical visible output with no extra static rebuilds; moving one
piece inside its chunk triggers exactly one static rebuild; the cutaway cache returns the
same Set object for a stationary player and recomputes after the player moves a tile or a
piece moves. Updated `packages/render/test/assets.test.ts` and
`packages/render/test/modular.test.ts` cutaway tests to numeric keys (the latter was caught
by typecheck, not by the test run). Headless bench
`packages/render/test/adr381_prepare_bench.test.ts` (PERF=1 only) measures `prepare()` by
scene plus both flood-fills directly; a standalone 5-batch BFS bench
(`adr381_bfs_bench.test.ts`) is included for the same measurements in isolation.
Typecheck clean with lockfile-pinned TypeScript 5.9.3 (`@engine/render` and
`@engine/client`, both EXIT 0). Render suite: 498 passed, 2 skipped, 0 failed (75 files).
Client suite: 861 passed, 9 failed (10 files failed of 187) — all 9 failed tests and the
3 file-level failures (adr216_lights, adr274_medical_icons, adr277_status_atlas, ENOENT
at import) are missing-art-file / art-count assertions in this sparse checkout (ENOENT
`ui_atlas.json`, `pets_dog_lab.png`, `items_build.png`, `render_tuning.json`; 705 audio
files without m4a twins; atlas-cell and fragment-key assertions against files the sparse
tree lacks). Proven pre-existing, not regressions: the same 10 files run isolated on
pristine fail a DIFFERENT set — 7 tests, all in adr242_art_fill — because pristine is a
FULL checkout (it has `pets_dog_lab.png` and `items_build.png`; the sparse tree does not)
while the working copy is sparse, so the art-test failure sets track the checkout, not
the code; and none of the failing tests imports the changed modules (the only shared
import is the `@engine/render` package index, and every failing assertion is about files
on disk). The patched failures reproduce identically isolated and in the full suite
(stable, not flaky). The gate's earlier server+client run had the same 9-failure count
from the same class.

**Not changed.** No graphics-quality change; no new art; no gameplay/balance change; no wire
change; the visible output of an unchanged world is bit-identical (asserted by test); the
static cache keeps `resolvePiece` running per frame (single-stage cache — skipping it would
need entry-stored resolve outputs plus fire/swing state in the signature, too risky for the
extra ~10–20%); the cutaway keeps its pre-existing one-frame cover lag (the cut reads last
frame's cover, because `gatherPieces` rebuilds the cover after the cut is computed).

**Honest cuts.** The bench is a stub-atlas, stub-GL headless measure on this VM — its absolute
ms are not phone ms; only the split and the patched-vs-pristine deltas are evidence, and VM
noise is ±30–50%, so only large deltas are claimable. The stub `resolvePiece` understates
the production resolve cost (real page/texture work), so the bench over-weights the cached
slice/hash work relative to production. No live visual verification was possible here:
Tracey's eyes on the live build are still the real check, including a fresh `?diag=1` after
the fix to see the new phase split (prep vs sprites vs upload vs lights) on her A16.

## ADR-382: Time-sliced abandoned stamping, redesigned — plan now, place N per tick, with the AI-visibility fixes (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** ADR-378 introduced time-sliced abandoned stamping (plan ~0.1 ms on chunk load,
place ≤20 pieces/tick via a postSim pump) and measured a real win: site-tick
`chunks.update()` p95 18.84→10.11 ms. The gate reverted it because it deterministically
broke 4 AI-human tests that passed before it: adr203 (campfire never built before night)
and adr252 block 2 ×3 (bots finish the pit but not the raised pad; don't build the 2×2
base/hearth/bed; never sleep in bed). The gate's experiments ruled out slicing spread
(cap 20→100000 still fails), pump registration, ruins existing, claim-target, node
clearing, placed-piece set (byte-identical), and footprint blocking — and two gate fixes
(boot drain + drain while tick<60) fixed adr203 but not adr252. This ADR is the redesign:
root-cause the failure first, then reintroduce the slicing with the AI-visibility fixes
that make it safe. ADR-378's code is reintroduced (its DECISIONS.md entry was reverted
with it, so this entry is the record); the two correctness fixes below are new.

**Root cause — two distinct failure modes, both proven by intervention, not by guessing.**

*Failure mode 1 — adr252 (raised pad never dug): the `editIndex`-gated pathfinder.*
`goTo()` in `packages/gameplay/src/ai/base_behaviors.ts` used the pathfinder
(`walkerWaypoint`) only when `editIndex(w).size > 0` — only after at least one terrain edit
existed in the world — and otherwise walked directly at its target with no obstacle
avoidance. (The same gate sat on the door path and in `travel.ts`'s `waterGate`.) The pad
bot's quarry stand is directly behind its own campfire (campfire at (-131.5,-135.0) sits
between the bot at (-130.7,-134.8) and the stand at (-134.5,-135.5)), and the campfire's
tile is solid for the body (`bodyAxisMove`/`edgeAxisMove`/`solidCell` — the centre-point
`movementBlocked` check returns false because it only tests the destination tile, which
is why the gate's footprint probe missed it). Traced over 3,600 pumps, deterministic:
in the pre-378 world the pit bot digs its pit early (~tick 600), creating the first
`TerrainEdit`, so `editIndex` is non-empty and the pad bot's `goTo` routes around the
campfire, reaches the stand, and the pad completes ~tick 1800. In the 378 world the
ruin-timing shift delays the first terrain edit until ~tick 2700, so `editIndex` stays
empty through the window when the pad bot needs the pathfinder; the pad bot walks
directly into its campfire, cannot move for ~60 ticks, `stuckOn` fires
(`stuckCount` 1→2, `workFail:1502`), `base_work` is suppressed (120-tick cooldown), and
the `travel` behaviour takes over and walks the bot 150 tiles away to (-75,-279), where it
stays — pad never dug, base/hearth/bed never built, bot never sleeps. The first dig
itself needs the pathfinder, so the gate was a circular dependency the pre-378 world only
escaped by lucky timing. Proof: removing the `editIndex(w).size` gate in `goTo` (one line,
in the 378 tree) makes all 4 adr252 block-2 tests pass; restoring the gate makes the new
`adr382_goto_routes_around_structures` regression test fail (and removing it makes it
pass). The cap=100000 experiment did not rule out timing: even with the cap, the pump runs
in postSim after `server.chunks`, so ruin pieces/markers still appear one tick later than
synchronous stamping — and the gate's drain only covered boot stamps and ticks < 60.

*Failure mode 2 — adr203 (campfire ~50% slower, past the 4800-tick bound): boot-stamp
timing.* The campfire test has a tight bound (pre-378 fire at ~4741 ticks vs the 4800
bound — 59 ticks of margin), and the 378 delay makes the bots ~2400 ticks slower
(fire ~7141). The `goTo` fix alone does NOT fix adr203 (still 1 failed with the gate
removed): the bots' early gather/claim/campfire decisions happen while boot-area ruins
are still assembling, so the world state they decide against differs from the synchronous
world. The gate's drain (drain boot stamps synchronously in `createGame` + while
tick<60) fixed adr203 3/3. Proof in the 378 tree: `goTo` fix + boot drain → adr203 3/3
pass. So the two fixes together are the complete set: the `goTo` fix removes the
adr252 failure mode, the boot drain removes the adr203 failure mode.

**Design.** Three parts, all in this ADR.

1. *Slicing (reintroduced from ADR-378, unchanged in mechanics).* `stampAbandonedSite`
plans (~0.1 ms) and enqueues; the postSim pump (`gameplay.abandonedStamps`, registered in
`install.ts`) places at most `stampPiecesPerTick` (data knob in
`packages/gameplay/data/abandoned.json`, leaf module `building/abandoned_data.ts`, default
20 ≈ 0.6–1.0 ms/tick at the measured 30–50 µs per placed piece) per tick, so a site
appears over ~3–10 ticks instead of one 4.5–9.2 ms hitch. Pieces land in the old order
(level, then PHASE: deck → wall → opening → stair → furniture/loot/fence/garden → roof),
the loot stream is consumed in placement order (a sliced stamp fills exactly the loot a
synchronous stamp would), and the marker (`AbandonedSite`) is only created when the site
completes (`finishStamp` clears footprint nodes, then creates the marker), so reclaim /
nearby-work / AI claim flows never see a half-built site. A second stamp for the same
origin while one is pending returns the pending handle; a chunk that unloads mid-stamp is
rolled back on the next pump tick; a server restart mid-stamp resumes from the placed
pieces (`matchPartialStamp`) instead of leaving a permanent half-ruin. The queue lives in
a module `WeakMap` keyed by `World` (no persistence/schema impact). One known quirk,
carried over: the sliced pump places 3 MORE pieces than synchronous stamping in two
kinds (Manor +1 L1 floor, Inn +1 L1 floor + storage box), because `snapPlacement` reads
the `StructureIndex`, which `structureIndexSystem` refreshes only during `world.step`'s
sim phase — synchronous stamping validates against a stale index and drops a few
plan-faithful pieces. The 3 extra pieces are plan-faithful, not a defect; the placed-piece
sets were byte-identical in the gate's 558-piece comparison of the worlds that matter.
2. *`goTo` always routes (the root-cause fix).* The `editIndex(w).size` gate is removed
from `goTo`'s main path and door path (`base_behaviors.ts`) and from `waterGate`
(`travel.ts`). `walkerWaypoint` already returns the direct goal when the ray is clear
(`navNeeded`), so the gate saved nothing but correctness. This makes AI movement robust
to any timing shift in when the world changes, not just this one.
3. *Boot drain (the adr203 fix, now a designed part of the slice, not a gate hack).*
`drainAbandonedStamps(world)` runs in `apps/server/src/game.ts` after the boot chunk
drain loop (before the first tick) and in `step` while `world.tick < 60`, so stamps for
chunks loaded before the first tick complete synchronously and the AI's early decisions
see the same world as synchronous stamping. The boot drain is load time, not frame time;
in-play stamps stay sliced, which is the hitch that matters for smoothness.

*Consequence of part 2 — mount-policy clearance probe (ADR-321).* Always routing changed
what `dismountReason` sees: with direct walking the rider's move vector pointed at its
goal, so the clearance probe (1 tile ahead along the move vector) saw a doorway the horse
could not pass and dismounted for "clearance". With pathfinding the move vector is a
detour around the doorway, so the probe missed it, the rider rode on, and the nearby
base-return goal (4.5 tiles away, `arriveTiles` 4) made it dismount as "arrived" instead
— `adr321_ai_mounts` "dismounts at a doorway" failed (expected "clearance", got
"arrived"). Fixed in `mount_behaviors.ts`: `dismountReason` now also probes toward the
goal (`tripGoal`) as well as the move direction. With direct walking the two coincide, so
this restores exactly the probe the old code made; with pathfinding it adds the
goal-direction probe the detour displaced. The donkey (fits the doorway) and the
"building" cases are unaffected (`rideClearanceBlocked` is species-aware; the building
check is separate). Verified: `adr321_ai_mounts` 15/15 pass.

**Tests.** New: `packages/gameplay/test/adr382_stamp_timeslice.test.ts` (renamed from the
378 file — slicing mechanics: per-tick cap, identical final site + loot vs synchronous,
drain, rollback on unload, resume after restart) and
`packages/gameplay/test/adr382_goto_routes_around_structures.test.ts` (a campfire directly
on the straight segment, zero terrain edits, and the bot must still reach the goal by
routing around it — fails with the old gate, passes with the fix). The 4 AI-human tests
are the acceptance gate and all pass with this ADR applied: adr203 3/3, adr252 block 2
4/4. Existing abandoned tests call `drainAbandonedStamps` after `stampAbandonedSite` so
their assertions see the completed site (11 files, one line each).

**Measurements.** Temporary vitest bench, same harness as ADR-378: real server wiring
(`ChunkManager` + `ProceduralGenerator` + `attachWorldStreaming`), vehicle speed 2.39
chunks/s at 20 Hz, 600 ticks, seed 1234, loadRadius 2, maxLoadsPerUpdate 4; 2 bench runs
per side (each 3 internal runs), process-CPU ms (not wall), median-of-medians. Identical
harness both sides: 376–379 chunks loaded, 33 sites, 33 site-ticks, 0 pending at end.

| metric (process-CPU ms, median of 2 runs) | before (sync stamp) | after (ADR-382) | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| site-tick `chunks.update()` median | 7.39 | 1.97 | −73% |
| site-tick `chunks.update()` p95 | 15.76 | 5.00 | −68% |
| site-tick tick-total (`update` + `world.step`) median | 10.65 | 3.65 | −66% |
| site-tick tick-total p95 | 21.13 | 10.96 | −48% |
| plain-tick `chunks.update()` median / p95 | 0.02 / 2.70 | 0.02 / 2.54 | unchanged |
| plain-tick tick-total median / p95 | 1.33 / 4.69 | 1.69 / 5.25 | pump slices land here now |
| all-tick tick-total median / p95 | 1.41 / 7.63 | 1.84 / 5.60 | hitch moved, not added |

Reading the table: the stamp cost left `chunks.update()` on site ticks (median −73%, p95
−68%) and now lands as bounded ≤~1 ms slices inside `world.step` on the following ticks
(plain-tick total median 1.33 → 1.69 ms — the cost spread out, not added: all-tick total
p95 actually fell 7.63 → 5.60, while the all-tick median rose 1.41 → 1.84 because the
median tick now carries a slice). No speedup is claimed for total chunk work — the same
chunks load and the same pieces place, spread over more ticks; that is the point. (The
absolutes are lower than ADR-378's bench because ADR-379's 2 ms chunk-load budget is
active in this harness, capping loads per update; the before/after delta is what is
comparable, and it is larger here because the budget and the slicing compound.)

**Not changed.** No gameplay, balance, or tuning values changed (SITE_CHANCE stays 0.15,
piece counts and loot unchanged — only the timing moves); no graphics-quality change; no
new art; no wire change. The boot drain is the only synchronous-stamp path, and it runs
at load time / in the first 60 ticks, not during play.

**Honest cuts.** The bench is a headless VM measure (process-CPU ms, no rendering, no
players, no network) — its absolute ms are not phone ms; only the before/after delta on
the identical harness is evidence, and VM noise is ±30–50% on p95s (the two before runs'
site-tick update medians were 6.97 and 7.80; the two after runs' were 2.07 and 1.87), so
only the large median deltas are claimable. The site-tick residual (~2 ms median in
`update()`) is terrain + node spawning + the ~0.1 ms plan, not the stamp. No live visual
verification was possible here: Tracey's eyes on the live build are still the real check,
including a fresh `?diag=1` after the fix — the new-area hitch should be visibly smaller,
and the boot split / phases line will show whether the remaining costs moved. The
`goTo` change makes every AI `goTo` call run the pathfinder's `navNeeded` check (a ray
cast + index query) even on pristine maps; the route search itself is still cached and
only runs when nav is needed, and the repo bench spread was not measured for this slice
(the 374–381 gate's spread median was 18.95 ms/tick; a re-measure at gate time would
confirm no regression). The `dismountReason` goal-direction probe adds one
`rideClearanceBlocked` call per mounted tick; it is the same cheap segment check the
move-direction probe already does.

## ADR-383: Lakes above sea level — elevated (mountain / perched) lakes (SurVivaZ)

**Context.** Tracey asked for lakes that sit above sea level: a water body in a bowl of higher terrain,
held by surrounding higher ground. There is no `seaLevel` / `SEA_LEVEL` constant anywhere in the code —
"sea level" is an emergent convention, not a value: the biome water band (noise < 0.3) plus the ADR-182
rule that every natural water tile renders at one flat surface, `WATER_SURFACE_HEIGHT = 0`
(`renderTileHeight` in `packages/world/src/waterDepth.ts`). So "above sea level" means a lake whose
rendered water surface is a level L > 0 while ordinary lakes and seas stay at 0.

**Design — reuse the existing water systems, do not invent a second one.** Every behaviour an elevated
lake needs already exists for one of the two existing water kinds, and this ADR is the combination:

- *Placement:* the ADR-255 forced-feature layout (`waterFeatureLayout`, pure function of seed) gains one
  `elevatedLake` per 512-tile region — centre, radius 6..10, surface level 4..7, on one of the two
  cardinals neither the lake nor the pond uses, at distance 84..104 (inside `WATER_FEATURE_RADIUS`).
  `waterFeatureAt` reports `"elevatedLake"` for disc tiles (precedence over lake/pond/river, so a river
  crossing the disc is swallowed by the lake and resumes at sea level either side). Deterministic and
  streamable exactly like the existing lake: chunk generation stays a pure function of (seed, tx, ty),
  and the disc + rim never reach the ±120 feature-window edge (max extent 104+10+4 = 118).
- *Surface height:* the ADR-263/297 flow-water encoding (`flowWaterRaw(level)` in the stored height
  byte) is the codebase's existing per-tile water-surface mechanism — it is how a shovel-dug channel
  keeps its own level. Elevated-lake water tiles store `flowWaterRaw(level)`, so with zero renderer
  changes `renderTileHeight` returns the elevated level, `terrainLevel` returns it, and
  `waterSurfaceAt` (terrain.ts, the flow system's source check) reads it. Both ground renderers
  (`render/src/tilemap.ts`, `render/src/terrainTiles.ts`) and the client's swimmer height
  (`apps/client/src/view.ts`) already draw through `renderTileHeight`; a render test pins
  `tileHeight` at the elevated level over the disc and 0 over the ordinary lake. The chunk codec
  stores heights as signed bytes (flow raw 84..87 fits), and a codec round-trip test pins it.
- *The bowl:* `heightFromNoise` shapes the terrain around the disc — inside the disc the bed sits at the
  surface level; a 1-tile beach shelf around it is clamped to [level+1, level+3]; beyond the shelf the
  rim only ever raises ground to level+1, out to 4 tiles, and natural hills resume. The shelf clamp is
  load-bearing for movement: `terrainStepBlocked` (terrain-ladder.ts) blocks upward steps over
  `MAX_UNAIDED_CLIMB = 3` unless a ladder spans the face, while descents are free — so a swimmer can
  always climb out of the lake onto the shelf (rise ≤ 3, and a 1..3 drop into the water costs no fall
  damage), and the water never sits above its shore. A test asserts every land tile touching the lake
  is climbable from the water (rise ≤ 3) for 40 seeds.
- *Behaves like a normal lake:* the lake is tile 1/8 water, so everything that routes through tile ids
  or depth needs no change and is tested for parity, not assumed: `waterDepthAt` (deep centre, shallow
  shore where a land shore exists), swimming (`swimTiles [1, 8]`), wetness / thirst / exposure
  (`inWater`, tile-based), AI water crossing (`water_crossing.ts` — the same ford/swim/around rule
  governs the elevated profile and the ordinary-lake profile, asserted rule-for-rule), and the flow
  system (a dug channel below the rim floods from the elevated lake, because `waterSurfaceAt` reads
  its surface — the dam-breach behaviour falls out of the existing code). Fishing and disease hooks:
  there are none to wire — no fishing system exists (`fish_shoal` is a sand-band resource node) and
  `diseases.ts` has no water hooks; anything tile-based includes the lake automatically.
- *What is NOT true:* `Transform.z` is the building-floor height, not terrain height (ground level is
  always z ≈ 0), so the swim-anim / no-sprint-while-swimming / loot-float checks (`z < 0.5`) work
  unchanged at an elevated surface. The lake does not drown spawn points (cardinal vs diagonal
  quadrants; tested). `heightAt` reports the surface level inside the disc (matching `terrainLevel`
  of the loaded chunk) while `sampleAt` returns the stored flow raw (matching the chunk byte) — the
  preview test's `sampleAt == chunk` contract is preserved, and `worldPreviewSvg` now shades by
  decoded terrain level so the raw 80+ byte does not paint a white halo on the shore pixels.
- *Knobs:* `ProceduralOptions.elevatedLakes` (`false` = off; otherwise `{minLevel, maxLevel, minRadius,
  maxRadius, minDistance, maxDistance, rimWidth}`, defaults 4..7 / 6..10 / 84..104 / 4). Production
  constructs the generator with `{ seed }` only, so the defaults are the live values; threading
  `worldgen.json` through would mean reordering server boot (the generator is built before defs load)
  and was left out rather than adding dead config.

**Measurements (headless VM, tsx, medians — no phone ms).** Chunk-load cost, before vs after on the
identical harness (88 chunks, 7 runs, fresh generator per run): before median-of-medians 4.49 ms/chunk
(run medians 4.00..4.82), after 4.28 ms/chunk (run medians 4.12..4.85 excluding the warmup run) — ranges
overlap completely, no regression shown, no speedup claimed. (Absolutes are VM tsx numbers, not the
~0.75 ms/chunk quoted for built loads.) Bowl survey over 200 seeds: 0 violations — shelf land always in
[level+1, level+3], outer rim always ≥ level+1, disc surface always exactly the elevated level.

**Tests.** New: `packages/world/test/adr383_elevated_lakes.test.ts` (12 tests: layout, surface, bowl,
climb-out, depth, spawn safety, survey, off-switch, far regions, preview decode),
`packages/gameplay/test/adr383_elevated_lakes.test.ts` (3 tests: AI crossing parity, flow surface),
`packages/render/test/adr383_elevated_lakes.test.ts` (1 test: tileHeight). Full suites, serialized,
TMPDIR under ~/workspace: world 91 passed, render 506 passed + 2 skipped, gameplay 2,091 passed +
3 skipped, client 895 passed — 0 failed anywhere. Typecheck EXIT 0 all 11 projects (lockfile-pinned
TypeScript 5.9.3).

**Honest cuts.** In ~32% of seeds (64/200) biome sea water touches the elevated disc, and in ~5% (23/500)
the lake has no land shore at all (it merges with a sea). There the raised disc sits in flat sea water
and the L-vs-0 step renders exactly like existing shovel-dug flow water — flat quads at different
heights with no side faces (`terrainTiles.ts` draws no drop edges for water) — so it reads as a raised
water plateau, not a bowl. That is a cosmetic edge, not a trap: water is traversable, and where a land
shore exists it is always climbable. Fixing it properly would mean noise-aware siting (choosing the
lake's cardinal by the height field, not by hash), which duplicates the biome formula into the layout
and was judged out of scope for this slice; it is the natural follow-up if Tracey finds the sea-merged
lakes ugly. No live visual verification was possible here: Tracey's eyes on the live build are the real
check — the lake should read as water sitting visibly higher than the surrounding sea, ringed by a
raised shore. No graphics-quality change; no new art; no input changes; no wire change; no gameplay,
balance, or tuning values changed beyond the feature itself.

## ADR-384: All abandoned structures built on one tile level (SurVivaZ)

Tracey asked that no abandoned structure be built across two different tile levels: every
ruin's ground footprint must sit on tiles of a single level. Two-story ruins keep their L1
(the rule is about the ground footprint's terrain level, not the building's floors).

What the code did before: `siteTerrainOk` (packages/gameplay/src/building/abandoned.ts) let a
footprint pass when `hi - lo <= maxSlope` (2, from building tuning in tiers.json), so a site
could straddle up to three distinct integer terrain levels and still stamp, its level-0
decks/walls/floors following the ground up and down inside one building. Per-piece placement
(building/place.ts) only checks slope per 1x1 piece, never per site — that was the gap.
Measured on real planned sites (ProceduralGenerator, 5 seeds): near region (chunks -10..10)
41.1% of planned sites were already single-level, 15.2% spread 1, 14.6% spread 2, 29.1%
spread 3+; far region (chunks 20..40) 38.6% single-level. All 28 kinds straddled (smallest
3x3 shed 24-34%, largest footprints 71-100%: homestead 83-85%, barn 75-86%, manor 71-100%).

Design (strict reject, no relocation, density compensation): `siteTerrainOk` is now exact —
`footprintSpread(world, ox, oy, w, h, 0) === 0`, early-exiting on the second distinct height
(~0.1 ms per straddling site against a live TileMap). A straddling site is SKIPPED in
`stampAbandonedSite` (a busy footprint still resumes in place via ADR-382's
`matchPartialStamp`, so a pre-384 partial stamp completes as-is — grandfathered, no
migration; already-stamped sites stay as-is). Player placement keeps its own maxSlope
tolerance; only abandoned sites are strict. Relocation was implemented first (spiral search,
radius 8, only for spread 1..2 sites the old gate would have stamped) and then REMOVED:
moving ruins deterministically broke the adr203 canary (no campfire near home in 4800
iterations, at both radius 8 and radius 4), while strict reject alone passes it (campfire
at tick ~3261, vs baseline ~3941). The mechanism was never isolated to a single ruin — no
relocated site sits near a bot base, and all four bots' paths diverge together after ~800
iterations (identical through 800, deterministic run-to-run) — so relocation is out and the
rule is enforced by skipping. Because the strict gate stamps only ~41% of planned sites,
`SITE_CHANCE` was raised 0.15 -> 0.25 so the realised density stays ~10 ruins per 100
chunks (0.25 x 0.41 ~= 0.15 x 0.71), the same world richness ADR-373 gave; the ADR-373
density test was updated to 0.25 / ~25 planned per 100 chunks. No levelling: there is no
terrain-levelling precedent in the codebase (terrain is only edited by players digging), so
the terrain is never rewritten to fit a ruin. `ai_spawn.ts` only reads `planAbandonedChunk`
(pure, unchanged) for AI spawn points beside seeded ruins — left unchanged; `claim_build.ts`
rebuilds already-stamped claimed ruins from the same plan — unchanged (grandfathered).
ADR-382 slicing is intact (plan ~0.1 ms, postSim pump <= 20 pieces/tick, marker only at
completion, rollback on unload, matchPartialStamp resume). No graphics change, no new art,
no wire change, no gameplay/balance/tuning change beyond the gate and the SITE_CHANCE
compensation.

Tests: new packages/gameplay/test/adr384_single_level_ruins.test.ts (9 tests): siteTerrainOk
exactness (flat passes, one tile up fails, water fails, no-terrain passes); a slope site is
skipped, not stamped straddling (spread 1, which the old gate passed); steep ground stays
skipped (no resurrection); flat ground stamps exactly where planned; all 28 kinds skip on a
slope and stamp flat on flat ground, never straddling; two-story kinds (TwoStoryCottage,
TwoStoryFarmhouse, Inn, Manor = 2 stories; Townhouse = 3) keep their upper floor on flat
ground and skip on a slope; chunk reload does not add a second site (standing site
grandfathered); chunk-load stamping skips a straddling site and stamps a flat one (real
ChunkManager + ProceduralGenerator, seed 1234); SITE_CHANCE compensation keeps realised
density near the old level (plan rate ~0.25, flat rate ~0.41, realised ~0.10/chunk).
Results: abandoned suites 17 files / 208 tests pass; canaries adr203 (3) + adr252-live (8)
= 11/11 pass, twice; typecheck EXIT 0 all 11 projects (pinned TS 5.9.3). No phone ms claimed;
no live visual verification was possible here — Tracey's eyes on the live build are the real
check that ruins sit flat. Known edge: a server restart mid-stamp plus a terrain change
under the site before reload could orphan the partial site (sub-second window, no crash);
a restart mid-stamp with unchanged terrain resumes it as before.

Gate fix (2026-11-13, gate commit 59aaffa): the 0.25 SITE_CHANCE compensation was REVERTED
to 0.15. The 0.25 reshuffles the site spawn-point set (planAbandonedChunk rolls sites at
SITE_CHANCE, and ai_spawn.ts reads the plan for bot respawn points), which deterministically
broke adr331 on seed 5: bot0 respawned at a site point (50,674) beside a terrain trap — a
resource node on a ridge it cannot climb (rise +6, max unaided climb 3) — and its goTo target
(43.5,681.5) stayed constant while its displacement stayed exactly 0.0 for the whole 120 s
window. The strict single-level gate alone (at 0.15) does NOT break adr331; only the 0.25
compensation does (verified: 384-only at 0.15 passes adr331 2/2). The freeze mechanism itself
is a pre-existing planner/pathfinder gap (the bot picks the nearest resource node without
checking reachability, and goTo falls back to walking directly at an unreachable target when
walkerWaypoint cannot route) — it is NOT fixed here. Trade-off of the revert: realised ruin
density is now ~0.06/chunk (~6 per 100 chunks) instead of ~0.10 — a visible reduction vs the
live game. Restoring 0.25 needs the planner/pathfinder to re-target unreachable resource
nodes (a new ADR). The ADR-373 density test and the ADR-384 density test were updated to
0.15 / ~15 planned per 100 chunks. The strict single-level gate itself is unchanged.

## ADR-385: Planner re-targets unreachable goals — bots stop freezing on ridges and behind their own walls (SurVivaZ)

Tracey asked for the real fix behind the ADR-384 gate revert: a bot that picks an
unreachable goal must re-target instead of freezing, so SITE_CHANCE can return to 0.25
and ruin density goes back to ~10 per 100 chunks. The gate's stated mechanism was
incomplete — the freeze it saw was not the gather sensor. Instrumented probes of the
seed-5 gate scenario (bot0 respawn (49.0,671.6), goal node (43.5,681.5) on a ridge at
height 14 vs the bot at 8, rise +6, max unaided climb 3) showed the freezing behaviour
was `garden`, not `gather`, on every sample: the unhired-bot `garden` behaviour runs
`farmRun` on `view.farm.harvest`, a wild berry bush picked by `computeFarmSensor` as
the nearest harvestable crop node within FARM_R (12) of the base anchor, with no
reachability check. `farmRun`'s stuck handling was `if (stuckOn(...)) return false;` —
no ban, no re-target — and the sensor re-reported the same bush every sense cycle, so
the bot froze for the full 120 s (displacement exactly 0.0, stuckCount 7 -> 42, the ban
map empty the whole time). The gather sensor has the same flaw (nearest node, no
reachability check), and `goTo` falls back to walking directly at an unreachable target
when `walkerWaypoint` cannot route — so the gap is in three places, all fixed here, and
the fix deliberately does NOT rewrite the pathfinder and does NOT change `goTo`'s
direct-walk fallback (it is transient — `waypoint()` re-plans on cache expiry — and
long-distance walking relies on it).

Design (narrow, fits existing systems): (1) a cached reachability predicate
`navReachable(world, e, x, y, gx, gy, goalLevel?)` in `systems/creature_nav.ts`,
right after `walkerWaypoint`: true when `navNeeded` is false (straight sight — the
ray checks terrain via `crossOk` -> `terrainMoveBlocked(..., avoidFalls=true)` plus
edge blockers and solid cells) or the cached route search reaches the goal tile
(`wp?.final`, else the nav-cache state's `reached` flag). It reuses the same cached
route `goTo` walks (cold check = one bounded A* with radius 24, maxNodes 1200,
detour 12; warm = cache read); callers must pass the walker's own current position —
reachability is positional. (2) Gather-node pick in `computeGoalSensors`
(`ai/autonomy.ts`) wrapped in a bounded retry loop (3 attempts, an `unreachable` skip
set): each attempt scans memory for the best-scoring node, checks `navReachable` from
the bot's own position, takes it if reachable, otherwise skips it and re-picks; no
gatherNode if none of the best 3 is reachable. New `isNodeBanned(bb, id, tick)` export
next to `banNode`. (3) Farm sensor: `computeFarmSensor` (`ai/hire_behaviors.ts`)
takes an optional `banned?` predicate; harvest candidates are collected (up to 4
nearest, in anchor-distance order, skipping banned ones) instead of taking the single
nearest, and the first candidate reachable from the bot's own position via
`navReachable` is picked (falls back to the nearest candidate if no Transform).
`fillHireSensors` passes the ban predicate at both `computeFarmSensor` call sites
(unhired-garden and Farm-job), built from the agent's bb via `isNodeBanned`. The
reachability check applies to harvest only — water/soil/till targets are base plots,
reachable by construction. `farmRun`'s harvest/tend branch now calls
`banNode(c, target.id)` on `stuckOn` before returning false, matching the existing
gather pattern. No new import cycles (`hire_behaviors` -> `creature_nav` is the same
direction as the existing `base_behaviors` -> `creature_nav` import; the autonomy <->
hire_behaviors cycle already existed via `stuckOn`).

SITE_CHANCE restored 0.15 -> 0.25 in `building/abandoned.ts`, and the two stale
in-code comments (:734, :820) that still described the reverted state now describe
the restored state. The ADR-373 density test is updated to 0.25 / ~25 planned per 100
chunks (1600-chunk bounds 340-460) and the ADR-384 density test to plan rate
(0.20, 0.30) and realised density (0.08, 0.13) (~0.10/chunk, ~10 per 100 chunks).

Two further pre-existing "walk directly at the target" stalls were found and fixed
while gating this change — both are the same class of bug (a straight-line distance
or a direct walk used where a wall intervenes), both proven by probe before fixing:
(4) `goTo` (`ai/base_behaviors.ts`) now returns the via-door path length, not the
straight-line distance, while the bot and its target are on opposite sides of the
bot's base wall (`dn + near->far + far->target`). Every caller uses `goTo`'s return as
"am I close enough?" (withdraw / craft / build / stash all stop on it); the straight
line understated the trip through the wall, so a bot standing inside 1.8 tiles from
an outside box stopped and tried the container through the wall. Once across, the
main path reports the straight line as before. (5) The `trip` behaviour's outbound
leg (`base_behaviors.ts`) used `toward` (a direct walk) instead of `goTo`, so a trip
that started while the bot was inside its base walked straight into the east wall and
never left: `toward` pushed it into the wall, `stuckOn` re-randomised the target every
120 ticks, and the trip monopolised the controller (it returns false every tick and
re-wins the think while `bb.trip` exists), starving `base_work` — the bot idled at
the bed withdraw forever and the ADR-252 live test failed (bot0 never built the bed).
The return leg already used `goTo`; the outbound leg now does too, so the bot exits
through the door and the trip can actually complete. The `goTo` return is the
via-door length while crossing, so the `< 2` arrival test still means "arrived" once
the bot is on the target's side.

Regression found during this work (ADR-252 live, seed 11, 2 bots, starters): the bed
step's withdraw stalled because bot0 ended up inside the base (standing at its own
campfire) while the storage box holding the bed's 6 planks is outside, east of the
base. On the base tree bot0 approached the bed stand from the north (outside) and the
test passed 8/8; on the ADR-385 tree the gather re-pick changed its path/timing so it
reached the withdraw step from inside, and the withdraw branch's straight-line
`goTo(...) > 2.2` check short-circuited the door routing. The fix is (4) + (5)
above — the withdraw branch itself is unchanged. Verified: adr252 live passes 8/8
three times in a row on this tree (it failed 2/2 before the fix, and the failure
reproduced with SITE_CHANCE temporarily back at 0.15, proving the sensor change —
not the density change — was the trigger).

Tests: new `packages/gameplay/test/adr385_unreachable_retarget.test.ts` (5 tests):
`navReachable` unit (ridge wall at x=13, +6 via `setTerrainDig`, spanning y -20..40;
the fixture installs a TileMap filled with tile 3 + `terrainFromTileMap`, as adr265
does, because `makeWorld()` installs no TerrainRes); gather re-pick (nearest tree on
the ridge top skipped, next reachable tree picked); no gather node when every
candidate is unreachable; farm sensor harvests the nearest reachable bush, not the
nearer ridge bush (`blueberry_bush` is a harvestable crop node); a banned harvest
target is never re-picked while the ban holds. New
`apps/client/test/adr385_unreachable_retarget.test.ts` (1 live test): replays the
seed-5 gate scenario (local server, seed 5, 3 bots; kill bot0, respawn far, hand back,
wait for route) and asserts max displacement > 8 tiles AND >= 2 distinct navGoals over
up to 120 s (breaks early when both are seen). On the fixed tree the bot re-targets
(navGoal changes every sample; displacement 0.0 -> 27.6 over 120 s; stuckCount stays
5 -> 8 instead of growing). Canaries: adr331 2/2 (repeat runs), adr203 campfire 3/3,
adr252 block-2 (gameplay file) 18/18, adr252 live 8/8 (x3).

Results (full suite, this tree): gameplay 2,105 passed; client 896 passed
(895 + 1 new live test); server 155; net 119; world 91; render 506; core 87;
input 74; persist 60 passed, 1 failed — the known autosave bench flake (passes
standalone with PERF=1; no ADR-385 file touches persist); assets 215; testkit 2.
Total 4,310 passed, 1 known flake, 0 regressions (gate5 total was 4,304; +6 = the
new tests). Typecheck EXIT 0 all 11 projects (pinned TS 5.9.3). No benches measured
(no hot paths touched beyond the sensor pick loops); no speedup claimed, no phone ms
claimed. No graphics change, no new art, no wire change, no gameplay/balance change
beyond the planner fix and the SITE_CHANCE restoration.

Known limits (follow-ups, not blockers): `navReachable` treats a CLOSED door as
solid (`solidCell`: a solid piece blocks unless it is a door AND `idx.doorOpen(c)`),
and it calls `waypoint()` directly, bypassing `goTo`'s door-aware branch (which
opens the door when crossing the bot's base wall) — so a goal across a closed door
reads as unreachable, and the gather/farm sensors skip it until the door opens.
Goals beyond the A* radius-24 window also read as unreachable on a one-shot check
(`goTo` handles far goals by walking partial routes and re-planning as the window
moves). Both err toward "skip and re-pick", which cannot freeze the bot; a
door-aware reachability check is a follow-up. The waterfall rule (ADR-386) is still
queued after this: elevated and sea-level lakes connect only via a waterfall, and
waterfalls do not exist yet.

## ADR-386: Waterfalls — elevated lakes never merge with the sea; the only connection is a waterfall (SurVivaZ)

Decision: noise-aware siting + a real waterfall feature. The hash layout is now only the
baseline: `siteElevatedLake` probes the BASE height field (`heightFromNoise(..., null, null)`:
no bowl, no spillway — no circularity, since the bowl only raises terrain) and picks the lake's
cardinal/position by it. Candidates are the two free cardinals (neither the lake nor the pond
uses them) at the hash distance and ±5/±10/±15/±20 tiles, all inside [84, 104] from the region
origin. Valid only when no biome sea lies within disc + 2 (disc + beach shelf + 1 land margin),
so every sited lake has a full land shore. Scoring is the MEAN base height in the shelf ring
(disc+1..disc+2), not the min — one low tile must not tank a direction. The hash placement
stands unless a challenger beats its mean by ≥ `SITING_HEIGHT_MARGIN` = 1 level. Fallback tier
if nothing in 84–104 is valid: distances [83, 78, 73, 68, 63] on the free cardinals (still
clear of the diagonal spawn patches and the lake/pond axes). No valid candidate →
`layout.elevatedLake = undefined`: the region is SKIPPED, never sea-merged.
`WaterFeatureLayout.elevatedLake` is now `{...} | undefined`; `elevatedLakeDist` returns
Infinity when there is no lake, and `elevatedLakeAt` / `waterFeatureAt` guard for it.
Unchanged: one lake per 512-tile region, radius 6–10, level 4–7, bowl + beach shelf clamped
[L+1, L+3] (rise ≤ 3 from the water, so a swimmer can always climb out).

`spillwayFor` runs for every sited lake. Target = nearest sea-level water (biome sea, or a
forced lake/river/pond at level 0) within `SPILLWAY_TARGET_RANGE` = 64 tiles beyond the rim,
found by ring scan. Breach = the rim tile (4-neighbour of a disc tile) closest to the target,
and among the near ones the lowest. Walk: 4-connected; each step keeps (or barely increases,
≤ +0.5) the distance to the target and takes the lowest ground among those steps; bounded by
`maxSteps = min(SPILLWAY_MAX_LEN = 64, 2×ceil(Euclidean breach→target) + 8)`; gives up when
boxed in, when it would leave the region's own span (`SPILLWAY_WINDOW` = 255), or past its
step budget. If the rim already touches lower water (a river passing the lake), no channel is
carved — the junction face itself is the waterfall. Channel levels: `tiles[0] = L−1`
(breach), `tiles[1] = L−3` (the waterfall — one 2-level drop), then −1/tile to a floor of 1,
running flat to the sea. Gate fix (length-1 spillways): a breach directly adjacent to lower
water would leave a 1-tile channel with no `tiles[1]` — no 2-level falls, just a 3..6-level
drop to the sea (fall damage going down, unclimbable back up). `spillwayFor` now returns
undefined when `path.length < 2`, treating those lakes as closed (15/2,000 seeds in the
gate's probe; the lake keeps its full land shore). Every spillway therefore has ≥ 2 tiles,
so the 2-level falls always exists. A 2-level drop is the steepest face that stays climbable/swimmable
both ways (MAX_UNAIDED_CLIMB is 3; drops ≤ 3 cost no fall damage via `terrainFallDamage`).
Encoding: spillway tiles are ordinary flow water (`flowWaterRaw(level)`), stored in `load()` /
`sampleAt()` like the disc. `forcedWater` includes spillway tiles (so `surface()` makes them
shallow tile 8 — fordable; a 1-wide channel always has land neighbours). `heightFromNoise`
consults the spillway before the bowl (the breach cuts the shelf); base-field probes skip it.
`layoutFor`'s non-zero-region window was extended from ±120 to the full 512-tile region span
(features sit within ±120, but a spillway may run to the region edge; region 0 already had no
cutoff; each tile belongs to exactly one region, so no overlap). Per-tile cost is fused into
one layout lookup via `lakeAndSpill()` (load/sampleAt thread the hold + spill level into
`heightFromNoise` as already-known, so it does not re-look them up).

Rendering (`packages/render/src/tilemap.ts`, `terrainTiles.ts`): the mesh renderer already
emits a water-coloured cliff face on every side whose neighbour is lower; the textured
renderer draws no side faces for water, so the mesh face is the visible face. New flags
`WATERFALL_PX..NY` = 6..9 (cliff flags 2..5 + 4), `WATERFALL_MIN_DROP` = 2,
`cliffFlagFor(water, normalFlag, topZ, neighbourLow)`: the waterfall flag only when the
neighbour exists (`NO_TILE_HEIGHT` = −99 never counts, so the view edge never shimmers) and
the drop is ≥ 2. Land cliffs never get it. `cliffShade` handles 6..9 (same shade as its cliff
normal). VS: waterfall faces (6..9) share cliff normals, collapse to `vFlags` 6, plus a new
`vZ` varying (tile height in levels). FS: `vFlags == 6` branch — bright streaks scrolling
DOWNWARD (smooth `vnoise`, `vZ * 1.5 + uTime * 1.0`), a sine band, foam flecks; excluded from
speckle, season tint, ice, puddles and snow (it does not ice over in winter — the flat water
does). No generated/faked art, no recolors, no reused sprites, no binary art: the falls are
runtime-painted shader water on the existing mesh face, exactly like the flat water's
animation. Textured skirt: water tiles get a skirt on sides whose neighbour is lower; zStep
is 16 px/level, so a 2-level falls face is 32 px and the 16 px skirt would hide its top
half — the skirt is now suppressed on waterfall faces (water tile, drop ≥
`WATERFALL_MIN_DROP` to an existing neighbour — imported from tilemap.js; no import cycle,
tilemap never imports terrainTiles). A 1-level ledge keeps its skirt (it covers the 1-level
mesh face, as before); a missing neighbour keeps its skirt (the mesh face there runs to the
void). Canvas2D (fallback renderer) draws no cliff faces at all, so the falls there read only
as a stepped stream.

Behaviour: waterfall tiles are ordinary flow water — swimming, wetness, fishing, water
depth, flow frontier all automatic; the channel reads Shallow (fordable) by the depth rule;
AI crossing treats it as a ford; the falls are passable both ways by swimming (2-level rise
≤ climb 3; going down costs no fall damage) — for every spillway, since all have ≥ 2 tiles
after the gate fix above. It connects the two water bodies; it does not
bar them. No particles (no waterfall sprite can be added without shipped art), no sound (no
sound hooks in gameplay). A one-way falls (unclimbable up) was NOT implemented — it would
need a water-landing fall-damage exemption + a climb rule; recorded as a follow-up.
Note: the junction face (a sited lake's rim directly touching a river/lake/pond at level 0,
18/490 = 3.7% of sited lakes) is the same one-way-trap shape as the length-1 spillway —
a 4–7 level drop with fall damage down and no climb back — and it is NOT fixed by the
length-1 guard. It predates ADR-386 (ADR-383 already let a river touch the disc) and is
queued as a follow-up: either step the junction down or treat it as barred/closed.
Feasibility probed with the fix: extending siting validity to also reject forced low water
within disc+2 would re-site 16 of the 18 junction lakes to a clean cardinal/distance and
skip 2 (skip rate 2.0% → ~2.4%); that is a siting-rule change, not a one-line guard, so it
stays queued rather than riding in the fix commit.

ADR-383 parity preserved: an elevated lake still behaves like a normal lake (same
ford/swim/around AI crossing rule, `waterSurfaceAt` reads the elevated surface, a dug channel
below the rim floods from it, chunk-boundary streaming intact, `sampleAt` agrees
tile-for-tile — tested: `load()` agrees with `sampleAt()` across the whole spillway, and the
codec round-trip preserves the flow-encoded channel levels). The ADR-383 ~5% no-land-shore
case is GONE for sited lakes: siting guarantees every sited lake a full land shore (0
no-shore lakes in 200 seeds; the skip is the escape hatch, not a merge).

Siting statistics (500 seeds, region 0): sited 490/500 (98.0%), skipped 10 (2.0%); moved
from the hash placement 409/490 (83.5%, mean move 84.3 tiles); with spillway/waterfall
235/490 (48.0%), closed lakes 255 (52.0%); spillway length mean 20.4, min 1, max 62;
sea-touch tiles within disc+2: 0; no-land-shore lakes: 0; rim touches a river/lake/pond
(junction face is the falls): 18 (3.7%); river crosses the disc: 0. [Gate fix, re-measured
on the fixed tree: with spillway/waterfall 234/490 (47.8%), closed lakes 256 (52.2%);
spillway length mean 20.5, min 2, max 62 — the one length-1 case in this 500-seed sample
is now a closed lake. 2,000-seed probe on the fixed tree: sited 1,964, with spillway 906,
0 length-1, tiles[1] correct on every spillway. All other buckets identical.] Far regions (120
samples: 40 seeds × regions [2,−1], [−3,2], [1,1]): sited 116 (96.7%), skipped 4 (3.3%),
with spillway 62 (53.4% of sited), sea-touch 0. 200-seed check: sited 197/200 (98.5%),
spillway 102/197 (51.8%). Skip justification (500 seeds): every skipped region's hash
placement itself touches the sea — the skip is a sea-merge avoided, not a siting failure.
Before the fallback tier, skips were 8.8%; the fallback rescued most (→ 2.0%). Dead ends
measured along the way: pure steepest-descent walk stalled on terrace plateaus (spill rate
1.7%); aiming at the nearest sea raised it to 32.8%; target-aware breach raised it to
47.8%; a `Manhattan + 12` step budget regressed it to 43.9% (mid-range targets need detour
slack — reverted to `2×Euclid + 8`, cap 64, giving 48.0–51.8%); shrinking the target range
64→48 cost ~4% (restored to 64).

Tests: 14 new ADR-386 tests (world 9, gameplay 2, render 3), all passing — siting across
200 seeds (zero sea-touch, radius 6–10, level 4–7, skip rate ≤ 5%, every sited lake has a
land shore), skip justification across 500 seeds, far-region siting, spillway structure
(4-connected, L−1 / L−3 / −1-per-tile to floor 1, end tile sea-level water 4-adjacent to the
last channel tile, only the last spillway tile touches sea, spillway presence ≥ 30% of
sited lakes), no flat merge anywhere, spillway Shallow/fordable with `load()` agreeing with
`sampleAt()`, `waterSurfaceAt` reading the descending surfaces, the falls drop climbable
both ways with no fall damage, `cliffFlagFor` unit tests, and a mock-GL mesh test (exactly
one waterfall quad, flag 6, on a hand-built 2-level water drop; a 1-level ledge, a land
cliff and a view-edge face stay plain cliffs). Gate-fix regression tests (world, +2): the
15 named length-1 seeds from the gate's 2,000-seed probe are closed lakes (spillway
undefined, lake still sited), and every spillway over a 2,000-seed sweep has ≥ 2 tiles
with `tiles[1]` at L−3 — the 200-seed structure sample could not see a 1.6%-of-spillways
defect, so the sweep is the probe as a test. ADR-383 tests updated to the sited layout
and passing (world 12/12, gameplay 3/3, render 1/1).

Gate fix (length-1 spillways; commit on top of 94be460): the gate's 2,000-seed probe found 15
length-1 spillways (1.6% of spillways) whose single breach tile dropped 3–6 levels straight
to the sea — fall damage going down, unclimbable back up, and the world test throwing on

the existing junction case), so those lakes are closed lakes. Regression tests (world, +2):
the 15 named seeds are closed lakes (spillway undefined, lake still sited), and a
2,000-seed sweep asserts every spillway has ≥ 2 tiles with `tiles[1]` at L−3. Re-measured
on the fixed tree: 500 seeds sited 490, with spillway 234 (was 235), spillway length mean
20.5, min 2, max 62; 2,000-seed probe sited 1,964, with spillway 906 (was 921), 0
length-1. Verification (fix tree): world 100 passed (98 + 2 new), gameplay 2,107 passed,
3 skipped, render 509 passed, 2 skipped; typecheck EXIT 0 all 11 projects (pinned TS
5.9.3); canaries adr203 3/3, adr252-live 8/8, adr331 2/2, adr385 live replay 1/1. Also
corrected with the fix: the ADR-386 entry's "min 1" / "passable both ways" claims, the

(candidates are scored by the MEAN shelf-ring height, not the lowest; distance steps are
±5/±10/±15/±20, not ±10/±20). The junction face stays queued (see Behaviour note above).

Results (full suite, this tree): gameplay 2,107 passed, 3 skipped; client 896 passed;

## ADR-387: Guide listings show their own icons; no sprint with a broken leg; the Guide's pages show a book, not emoji (SurVivaZ)

Decision: three parts, one ADR. (1) Every Guide listing shows the icon of the thing it
describes, derived from the fact it already resolves — no new data, no new art. (2) A player
with a broken leg cannot sprint: the shared movement path ignores sprint while `broken_leg`
is active. (3) The Guide's pages and entry buttons show a runtime-painted book icon; the
📖 emoji is gone from the Guide UI.

Guide icons (`packages/gameplay/src/guide.ts`, `guideFactIcon`, wired into
`resolvedGuideSection` so every resolved fact item carries `icon?: GuideRowIcon`). Three
shapes, rendered by the client (`apps/client/src/guide-panel.ts`, `factIconNode`): `guide`
(a `GuideIconRef`, a `[data-icon]` span through the same `guideIconKey` hook section icons
use); `condition` (a `diseaseIcon()` result, rendered through `conditionIconImg` — the HUD's
own status-art path); `file` (an embedded ic_ PNG, rendered through `iconImg`). Derivation,
first match wins: `diseases.<key>.durationSeconds|cure` -> the disease's own status icon
(`diseaseIcon`: broken_leg -> the dedicated UI-atlas `"broken_leg"` art, wound_infection ->
`"infected"`, common_cold -> `ic_snowflake.png`, influenza -> `ic_temp.png`, everything else
-> the generic `ic_health.png`) — the same icon the HUD disease chips show, so the guide and
the HUD agree about what ails you; `animals.treats.<species>` -> `pet:<species>`;
`mounts.<species>.*` -> `mount:<species>`; format `"item"` (and not a disease row) ->
`item:<the resolved item key>` (the harness, the coin); then the explicit `FACT_ICONS` map,
one row at a time — the piece the row is about (claim totem, campfire, ore/crop/salt stores,
stalls, feeding trough), the item the row is about (fur coat/hat, salt, rope), or an ic_ file
icon where that icon IS the row's subject (the backpack for the inventory rows, the fire for
the fire rows, the snowflake/thermometer for the freezing/heat rows, the plant for the crops
row, the HUD season icons for the summer/fall/winter rows). Coverage: 133 fact rows, 64 with
icons (18 file, 15 condition, 31 guide), 69 without — aggregate counts, durations, zombie
rates and the like describe a number, not a thing with art, and controls rows describe
keybindings. A row whose icon has no art renders text-only, never a placeholder. Fact icons
render at 20px before the label (`.guide-fact-label`); quick-jump buttons show their section
icon (24px, flex row); section headers are unchanged.

Book icon (`apps/client/src/guide-art.ts`): NEW pixels, painted at runtime with the Px
software canvas (Task 34 / ADR-361 pattern) — a closed red leather book, gilt frame and
medallion, cream page block on the right edge, dark spine on the left, gold bookmark ribbon,
128x128, pixel-checked by the ADR-387 client test. No sprite is reused for a different thing
and no binary art ships. `installGuideMenuIcon` registers the PNG in `ICON_DATA` under
